Author’s analytic distinctions: The authors ruled out bacterial sepsis (no bacterial growth, lack of response to antibiotics), viral opportunistic infections (CMV antigenemia negative, low PCR load, EBV not demonstrated), cryptococcosis (negative latex test), and tuberculosis (normal CT, no microbiologic evidence) while emphasizing mucocutaneous lesions, ulcerative esophagitis, high ferritin, and eventual isolation of Histoplasma from blood and skin biopsy.
case_prompt:
A 64‑year‑old woman, six years post renal transplantation, presented with a 36‑hour history of fever, hypotension, and asthenia accompanied by a 7‑kg weight loss over the preceding three months. Physical examination showed oral white plaques and a maculopapular rash on the back. Laboratory studies revealed anemia (Hb 8.4 g/dL, Ht 23 %), leukopenia (2.3 × 10⁹/L), elevated C‑reactive protein (10.8 mg/dL) and ferritin (13 253 ng/mL), and acute graft dysfunction (serum creatinine rising from a baseline of 3.0 mg/dL to >4.0 mg/dL). Liver enzymes were within normal limits. Immunosuppression consisted of prednisone 5 mg/day and azathioprine 2 mg/kg/day. 

On admission, blood cultures were obtained for fungi and mycobacteria. PCR assays for cytomegalovirus (CMV) and Epstein‑Barr virus (EBV), a latex agglutination test for cryptococcus, and serologies for Histoplasma capsulatum and Trypanosoma cruzi were ordered. Empiric therapy with vancomycin, meropenem, and ganciclovir was started to cover possible bacterial or viral opportunistic infection. CMV antigenemia was negative, but PCR detected 546 copies of CMV DNA. 

A skin‑lesion biopsy and fungal/mycobacterial cultures were performed. Thoraco‑abdominal CT scan and transthoracic echocardiogram showed no abnormalities. Bone‑marrow aspiration demonstrated erythroid hyperplasia. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy revealed ulcerative esophagitis with intranuclear inclusions and focal candidal plaques; fluconazole was added to the regimen. 

The patient’s condition deteriorated, developing melena, mucocutaneous bleeding, hemodynamic instability, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Empiric liposomal amphotericin B was initiated to cover histoplasmosis, and a four‑drug antitubercular regimen was started. She required mechanical ventilation, vasopressor support, and subsequently developed amphotericin‑related hepatotoxicity, culminating in death seven days after initiating antifungal therapy.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial sepsis considered due to fever, hypotension, leukopenia, and high CRP; empiric broad‑spectrum antibiotics started | "empiric treatment with vancomycin, meropenem, and ganciclovir was started aiming to treat a possible bacterial infection..."
2. Cytomegalovirus infection evaluated; PCR positive but antigenemia negative, indicating low‑level viremia insufficient to explain the fulminant picture | "CMV antigenemia was negative but PCR unveiled 546 copies of the virus."
3. Epstein‑Barr virus infection assessed; PCR performed but no positive result reported, making EBV an unlikely primary pathogen | "PCR for ... Epstein Barr virus (EBV) ... were also done."
4. Cryptococcosis screened with latex agglutination; lack of reported positivity argued against this diagnosis | "latex agglutination test for cryptococcus ... were also done."
5. Tuberculosis considered because of systemic symptoms; empirical four‑drug anti‑TB therapy begun despite normal thoraco‑abdominal CT and no microbiologic confirmation | "We empirically started ... a four‑drug treatment for tuberculosis."
6. Histoplasmosis suspected based on oral candidiasis, cutaneous rash, ulcerative esophagitis with intranuclear inclusions, marked weight loss, anemia, leukopenia, and markedly elevated ferritin; empirical liposomal amphotericin B was added to cover this infection | "We empirically started liposomal amphotericin B to cover histoplasmosis..."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s central diagnostic challenge is identifying the causative organism of the intra‑abdominal lymphadenitis in an HIV‑infected child. The organism ultimately identified is Mycobacterium genavense, which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases. The patient also has HIV infection (hiv_aids), a SELECTED disease, but it is known from the outset and is not the mystery to be solved. Therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.  
2. Breakpoint: Include all information up to the point just before the definitive molecular identification of Mycobacterium genavense (i.e., stop before “In May 2017, a diagnosis of Mycobacterium genavense was made…”). This provides the presentation, imaging, HIV status, initial laboratory work‑up, initial histology, AFB findings, negative TB/MAIC PCRs, and urinary LAM result—enough for learners to work toward the correct organism without revealing it.  
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished Mycobacterium genavense from Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Mycobacterium avium complex, lymphoma, and CMV disease by (a) histology showing non‑tuberculous mycobacteria, (b) persistent AFB on tissue despite negative cultures, (c) multiple negative PCR assays for M. tuberculosis complex and M. avium complex, (d) positive urinary lipoarabinomannan suggestive of disseminated mycobacterial infection, and (e) later molecular sequencing that confirmed M. genavense. They also considered IRIS and malabsorption as contributors to clinical failure, but those were managed therapeutically rather than as primary diagnoses.
case_prompt:
An 8‑year‑old boy from Limpopo, South Africa, with a history of premature birth, chronic undernutrition (weight‑for‑age z score = ‑2, BMI = 13), and a 2‑year history of abdominal distension, diarrhoea, night sweats and failure to thrive was referred to paediatric gastroenterology in October 2016. He had recent travel to Kruger National Park and India six months earlier. Vaccination history was reported as up‑to‑date, but not verified.

On admission he was acutely ill, severely wasted (17 kg), febrile (39 °C), pale, tachycardic and had mild lower‑limb oedema. Physical examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly without peripheral lymphadenopathy; the abdomen was markedly distended with recurrent diarrhoea and vomiting and food intolerance.

Abdominal CT and ultrasound showed massively enlarged intra‑abdominal lymph nodes with a “moth‑eaten” spleen and prominent collateral vessels suggesting portal hypertension.

Laboratory studies showed HIV infection with CD4 = 59 cells/µL (7%) and HIV viral load = 453 780 copies/mL. Mildly elevated transaminases, moderate proteinuria, fecal alpha‑1 antitrypsin consistent with protein‑losing enteropathy, and microcytic hypochromic anaemia with reticuloendothelial iron blockade were noted.

The initial differential diagnosis emphasized tuberculosis or lymphoma. Over 7 months, endoscopic and surgical biopsies of duodenal and lymph‑node tissue were obtained. Histology was interpreted as consistent with a non‑tuberculous mycobacterial infection.

Acid‑fast bacilli were identified on lymph‑node tissue (12 Oct 2016) and on a repeat biopsy (8 Mar 2017). Stool microscopy (26 Mar 2017) also revealed acid‑fast organisms with a coccoid appearance. PCR assays for Mycobacterium avium complex were negative, as were multiple PCR platforms for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex (Nanogen, BD MAX, Xpert MTB/RIF). Urinary lipoarabinomannan testing (22 Mar 2017) was positive.

A CMV viraemia of 3 974 copies/mL and a colon biopsy PCR positive for CMV were recorded in March 2017, as was an Epstein‑Barr virus load of 9 318 copies/mL.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Tuberculosis considered due to fever, weight loss, hepatosplenomegaly and intra‑abdominal lymphadenopathy; excluded because multiple PCR assays for the Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex were negative and cultures yielded no growth. | "Numerous PCR assays for Mycobacterium tuberculosis complex were negative... Mycobacterial cultures, all of which showed no growth."
2. Lymphoma considered because of massive intra‑abdominal lymphadenopathy and systemic symptoms; excluded by histology showing non‑tuberculous mycobacteria rather than malignant cells. | "The findings were consistent with non‑tuberculous mycobacterial infection."
3. Mycobacterium avium complex (MAC) considered given HIV immunosuppression and AFB positivity; excluded by a negative PCR assay for MAC. | "The polymerase chain reaction (PCR) assay for Mycobacterium avium complex was negative."
4. Cytomegalovirus disease considered due to CMV viraemia and positive colon biopsy; deemed a co‑infection rather than the primary cause of the abdominal lymphadenopathy, as histology did not reveal CMV cytopathic effect and the clinical picture persisted despite ganciclovir. | "A cytomegalovirus (CMV) viraemia of 3974 copies/mL... was measured... together with a colon biopsy that was PCR positive for CMV."
5. Disseminated non‑tuberculous mycobacterial infection remained likely because AFB were repeatedly seen in tissue and stool, urinary LAM was positive, and all specific mycobacterial PCRs were negative, indicating an atypical organism. | "Acid‑fast bacilli (AFB) were noted during the processing of the tissue samples... The urinary lipoarabinomannan test... was positive."
6. Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) was contemplated after ART initiation due to clinical worsening despite virologic suppression; however, lack of improvement after corticosteroid therapy suggested ongoing infection rather than pure IRIS. | "Immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS) was considered, and methylprednisone was initiated..."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately identifies a de‑novo heterozygous SAMD9 mutation causing a bone‑marrow‑failure/immunodeficiency phenotype, which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases. Therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.  
2. Breakpoint: Include all clinical and laboratory data up to (but not including) the paragraph that announces the discovery of the SAMD9 mutation. This provides the immunologic phenotype, CMV viremia, lymphocyte subset abnormalities, functional assays, and the negative work‑up for other known genetic causes, allowing students to formulate a differential before the definitive genetic result.  
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors systematically excluded congenital neutropenia, dyskeratosis congenita, and classic SCID by negative gene panels, normal early TREC/KREC levels, and later‑onset decline; they highlighted persistent CD8 activation with CMV, reduced lymphocyte proliferation, and finally demonstrated a gain‑of‑function effect of the novel SAMD9 variant in vitro to support the diagnosis.
case_prompt:
Whole‑exome sequencing performed at 18 months failed to reveal mutations in genes associated with congenital neutropenia or dyskeratosis congenita, which were initially considered because of a presumed Hoyeraal‑Hreidarsson syndrome. No other potentially causative variants were identified using a virtual panel of genes linked to bone‑marrow failure or immunodeficiency.

Immunologic testing summarized as follows. Flow cytometry first performed at 5 months showed a markedly increased proportion of CD3⁺ T cells (87–96 % of lymphocytes; absolute 2.99–9.88 × 10⁹ L⁻¹) with normal CD4 counts (21–42 %; 1.34–2.28 × 10⁹ L⁻¹) and markedly elevated CD8⁺ cells (47–69 %; 1.62–7.49 × 10⁹ L⁻¹). CD19⁺ B cells were profoundly reduced (≈2 %; 0.07–0.22 × 10⁹ L⁻¹). NK cells were within normal limits. Immunoglobulin levels were elevated (IgG 10.6 g/L, IgM 7.1 g/L) with later normalization of IgG and IgA and a decline of IgM to 3.25 g/L; IgE remained <17 IU/mL. Total hemolytic complement (CH50) and the granulocyte burst test were normal.

At 7 months, detailed flow cytometry revealed strong CD8 activation (HLA‑DR⁺ 72 %) with a shift from naïve (6 %) to effector‑memory phenotype (77 %). Persistent CMV viremia was documented, yet functional CMV‑specific T cells were absent; a minor CD8⁺ IFN‑γ⁺ response was noted at 8.5 months but did not clear the virus until one year of age, when PCR became negative. Neonatal dry‑blood‑spot testing was negative for CMV.

Lymphocyte proliferation to phytohemagglutinin was repeatedly reduced between 5 and 14 months. At 7 months, activated T‑cell cultures (anti‑CD3ε + IL‑2) showed reduced viability, absent Bcl‑2 expression, and slightly decreased calcium flux after TCR stimulation, while overall tyrosine phosphorylation was unchanged. Six months later, after CMV control, these functional defects normalized.

T‑cell receptor excision circles (TREC) and kappa‑deleting element excision circles (KREC) were not decreased at 5 months, but at 17 months KREC numbers fell to levels typical of SCID patients and TREC fell below the 3rd percentile.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Congenital neutropenia considered because of early‑onset cytopenias, but whole‑exome sequencing excluded mutations in known neutropenia genes. | "Mutations in the genes causing congenital neutropenia were excluded..."
2. Dyskeratosis congenita (Hoyeraal‑Hreidarsson syndrome) entertained due to immunodeficiency and growth failure, yet no pathogenic variants were found in associated genes. | "...as well as variants in genes causing dyskeratosis congenita, because Hoyeraal Hreidarsson syndrome was considered."
3. Classic severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) was a possibility given low lymphocyte proliferation, but early TREC/KREC values were normal and the decline occurred only later, arguing against primary SCID. | "Neither T‑cell receptor excision (TREC) nor kappa‑deleting element excision (KREC) circle levels were decreased at 5 months..."
4. Primary humoral immunodeficiency considered because of elevated IgM and reduced B cells, yet immunoglobulin subclasses later normalized and functional antibody responses were not described, making isolated humoral defect unlikely. | "IgG 10.6 g/L, IgM 7.1 g/L... CD19⁺ cells were markedly decreased..."
5. Persistent CMV infection was identified as a driver of CD8 activation, but CMV alone could not explain the broad T‑cell proliferation defect, the dynamic change in KREC/TREC, and the later normalization after viral control. | "Persistently present CMV viremia... CMV reactivation control was restored only at one year of age (PCR CMV negativity)."
6. Bone‑marrow‑failure syndromes other than SAMD9 (e.g., Fanconi anemia) were not supported by cytogenetic abnormalities or characteristic physical findings; genetic panels were negative. | "No other potentially causative variants were found using the virtual panel of genes associated with bone marrow failure or immunodeficiency."
7. Gain‑of‑function SAMD9 mutation ultimately explained the proliferative arrest, increased apoptosis, and necrosis seen in patient‑derived cells, fulfilling the pathogenic mechanism. | "Transient ectopic expression of wt SAMD9 resulted in a significant decrease in proliferation... mutant SAMD9 induced primary necrosis... demonstrating the gain‑of‑function impact of p.R824Q."

case_prompt:
A 26‑year‑old woman with a known history of HIV infection diagnosed at age 15 presented to the emergency department with a 10‑day history of intermittent lower abdominal pain, nausea, bilious vomiting, and asthenia. The pain worsened markedly 24 hours before admission. On examination she appeared dehydrated, hypotensive, and tachycardic. Her abdomen was diffusely tender with marked peritoneal signs. Laboratory studies showed mild leukocytosis with neutrophilia, and arterial blood gas demonstrated metabolic acidosis with hyperlactatemia.  

Given these findings, a surgical consultation was obtained and diffuse peritonitis was diagnosed. Aggressive crystalloid resuscitation was initiated and an emergency laparotomy performed. Intra‑operatively the peritoneal cavity contained approximately 500 mL of pus, and two bowel perforations were discovered: a 1 × 1 cm perforation in the terminal ileum 50 cm proximal to the ileocecal valve, and a 3 × 2 cm perforation in the cecum. A right colectomy was performed with a side‑to‑side ileotransverse anastomosis. Initial differential considerations, based on the clinical scenario, included intestinal perforation due to cytomegalovirus infection, mycobacterial infections, fungal infections, neoplastic disease, or Kaposi sarcoma. Pathology and HIV‑related laboratory testing were not immediately available.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Cytomegalovirus infection considered because HIV patients with low CD4 counts are predisposed to CMV colitis and perforation. | "Based on the historical, clinical, and laboratory data obtained, we initially considered intestinal perforation due to cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection as the probable etiology of peritonitis."
2. Mycobacterial infection (including tuberculosis) listed as a differential given the HIV context and bowel ulceration. | "...the differentials included, mycobacterial infections, fungal infections, neoplastic disease or Kaposi sarcoma."
3. Fungal infection entertained as a possible cause of bowel ulceration and perforation in severely immunocompromised hosts. | "...mycobacterial infections, fungal infections, neoplastic disease or Kaposi sarcoma."
4. Neoplastic disease (e.g., lymphoma) considered because abdominal masses can present with perforation. | "...mycobacterial infections, fungal infections, neoplastic disease or Kaposi sarcoma."
5. Kaposi sarcoma included as a potential intestinal lesion leading to perforation in advanced HIV. | "...mycobacterial infections, fungal infections, neoplastic disease or Kaposi sarcoma."
6. Tuberculosis confirmed by pathology showing chronic inflammation, multiple mucosal ulcers, and granulomas in bowel and lymph nodes, establishing it as the definitive cause. | "revealing chronic inflammation of the resected bowel, ... multiple granulomas ... Bowel perforation due to tuberculosis was confirmed as the final diagnosis."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient develops Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, which corresponds to “pneumocystis” on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. No other SELECTED disease is the primary focus of the presented work‑up.
2. Best breakpoint: Include all clinical data up to the performance of bronchoscopy but stop before reporting the bronchoalveolar lavage PCR result that identifies Pneumocystis. This gives students the presenting symptoms, laboratory abnormalities, immunologic profile, and CT imaging necessary to generate the differential and arrive at the diagnosis without explicit confirmation.
3. Analytic distinctions (from article): The authors used a combination of (a) characteristic CT pattern (diffuse ground‑glass opacities), (b) markedly elevated LDH, (c) severe hypogammaglobulinemia with B‑cell depletion after rituximab, and (d) extensive microbiologic work‑up that excluded bacterial, mycobacterial, viral (CMV, EBV) and fungal (Aspergillus, Cryptococcus) pathogens, thereby supporting Pneumocystis infection and ruling out other opportunistic pneumonias.
case_prompt: In May 2016, a 25‑year‑old woman was hospitalized after 15 days of low‑grade fever, weight loss, a non‑productive cough and progressive dyspnea. Laboratory studies showed a C‑reactive protein of 40 mg/L, lactate dehydrogenase of 340 U/L (reference 5‑240 U/L) and β2‑microglobulin of 3.53 mg/L (reference 1.2‑2.5 mg/L). Immunologic assessment revealed persistent hypogammaglobulinemia, absence of circulating CD19⁺ B cells, and a reduced peripheral CD8⁺ T‑cell count without evidence of CD4⁺ T‑cell activation (HLA‑DR negativity). Chest computed‑tomography demonstrated bilateral diffuse infiltrates, ground‑glass opacities and several large pulmonary nodules. A bronchoscopy with broncho‑alveolar lavage was performed to determine the etiology of the pulmonary infiltrates; the samples were sent for microbiologic and molecular testing.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial pneumonia considered because of fever and infiltrates, but cultures and broad‑spectrum antibiotics failed to isolate a pathogen and the CT pattern was atypical for bacterial consolidation. | "Searches for other pathogens, including Mycobacterium tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteria, cytomegalovirus, Cryptococcus and Aspergillus species, were negative."
2. Mycobacterial infection (TB or atypical) considered given immunodeficiency; excluded by negative acid‑fast stains, cultures and molecular assays. | "Searches for other pathogens, including Mycobacterium tuberculosis, atypical mycobacteria… were negative."
3. Viral pneumonias (CMV, EBV) considered; CMV PCR and EBV studies were negative, and no cytopathic changes were seen on cytology. | "Searches for other pathogens… cytomegalovirus… were negative."
4. Invasive fungal infection (Aspergillus, Cryptococcus) considered because of nodular lesions; serum galactomannan and fungal cultures were negative, and no hyphae were observed on broncho‑alveolar lavage. | "Searches for other pathogens… Cryptococcus and Aspergillus species, were negative."
5. Lymphomatous pulmonary involvement (DLBCL) considered given prior rituximab exposure; bronchoscopy biopsies later showed lymphoma, but at this point no infiltrative tumor cells were identified in BAL, making primary infection more likely. | "Bronchoalveolar lavage analysis… (pending) and no malignant cells were reported."
6. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia supported by (a) profound immunodeficiency with B‑cell depletion, (b) elevated LDH, (c) CT findings of diffuse ground‑glass opacities, and (d) eventual detection of Pneumocystis cysts on BAL PCR, confirming the diagnosis. | "Bronchoalveolar lavage analysis revealed Pneumocystis jiroveci cysts with positive polymerase chain reaction (PCR) (4,000 copies/mL)."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case centers on TAFRO syndrome, a severe variant of idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease, which is not listed among the 21 SELECTED diseases. therefore the final answer will be “TAFRO syndrome -> OUT_OF_SCOPE”.
2. Best Breakpoint: End the prompt after the cervical lymph‑node biopsy (day 10) showed mixed‑type MCD histology, but before the authors state “We suspected TAFRO syndrome…”. This provides all clinical, laboratory, and imaging data needed to formulate the diagnosis without revealing it.
3. Analytic Distinctions: The authors excluded HHV‑8 infection (PCR negative), other viral infections (CMV antigenemia not yet present), autoimmune Sjögren syndrome (lip biopsy non‑diagnostic, anti‑SS‑A isolated), malignancy (FDG‑PET no significant uptake), and typical causes of edema (cardiac, hepatic, renal) through imaging, serologies, and biopsy, leading them to the diagnosis of TAFRO syndrome.
case_prompt: A 46‑year‑old Japanese man with no notable past medical history presented with a two‑week history of fever, fatigue, progressive generalized edema, abdominal distention, and a 7‑kg weight gain despite poor oral intake. He denied prior infectious illnesses. On examination he appeared exhausted; temperature 37.8 °C, blood pressure 160/93 mmHg, heart rate 109 bpm, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO₂ 90% on room air. He had generalized pitting edema, weak basal lung sounds, hepatomegaly, and a distended abdomen; there was no jaundice. Laboratory studies revealed leukocytosis (14,600/µL), mild anemia (Hb 11.1 g/dL), thrombocytopenia (11.1 × 10⁴/µL), renal dysfunction (BUN 60.7 mg/dL, creatinine 2.94 mg/dL), CRP 14.25 mg/dL, ALP 768 U/L, polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia (IgG 2461 mg/dL) with an elevated IgG4 level (235 mg/dL). Autoantibody screening was negative except for ANA x40 and anti‑SS‑A antibody; HHV‑8 PCR in serum was negative. Contrast‑enhanced CT showed massive pleural effusions, ascites, mild generalized lymphadenopathy (<1.5 cm), and hepatosplenomegaly. Echocardiography demonstrated normal wall motion, no valvular disease, and a collapsed inferior vena cava (<5 mm). FDG‑PET revealed no significant uptake aside from slight uptake in para‑aortic nodes. Lip biopsy performed on day 6 did not meet criteria for Sjögren syndrome. Ophthalmologic exam showed marked bilateral optic edema without keratoconjunctivitis. Serum IL‑6 and plasma VEGF measured on day 9 were elevated (IL‑6 25.2 pg/mL, VEGF 224 pg/mL); ascitic fluid IL‑6 and VEGF were markedly high (IL‑6 3310 pg/mL, VEGF 335 pg/mL). Bone‑marrow aspiration yielded a dry tap; biopsy showed a mild increase in megakaryocytes and mild reticulin myelofibrosis. Cervical lymph‑node biopsy on day 10 demonstrated findings compatible with mixed‑type multicentric Castleman disease histology.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Infection by HHV‑8 (Castleman disease variant) was considered but excluded by a negative HHV‑8 PCR in serum. | "Polymerase chain reaction for HHV‑8 DNA in a serum sample was negative..."
2. Sjögren syndrome was entertained due to positive anti‑SS‑A antibody, yet excluded by non‑diagnostic lip‑biopsy findings. | "Considering the positive anti‑SS‑A antibody finding, lip biopsy was performed on day 6, but the pathological findings did not meet the criteria for Sjogren syndrome."
3. Other autoimmune disorders were ruled out because autoantibody screen was essentially negative aside from low‑titer ANA. | "Immunological screening test results for autoantibodies were negative, except for positive antinuclear antibody (x 40) and anti‑SS‑A antibody."
4. Malignancy (lymphoma, solid tumor) was deemed unlikely given the lack of FDG uptake on PET imaging. | "FDG‑PET revealed no apparent FDG uptake, except for slight uptake in the para‑aortic lymph nodes."
5. Cardiac, hepatic, and renal causes of edema were evaluated: normal cardiac wall motion on echocardiography, absence of jaundice, and only mild hepatosplenomegaly argued against congestive heart failure or advanced liver disease as primary drivers. | "Echocardiography performed on day 2 revealed normal wall motions without any sign of valvular disease... Jaundice was not observed, but a distended abdomen and hepatomegaly were observed."
6. The combination of thrombocytopenia, anasarca, fever, renal dysfunction, and lymphadenopathy, together with the mixed‑type Castleman disease histology, supported a diagnosis of TAFRO syndrome. | "Biopsy of a cervical lymph node was performed on day 10, and the pathological findings were compatible with a mixed‑type MCD histology... We suspected TAFRO syndrome..."

1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s final diagnosis is parvovirus B19‑induced pure red cell aplasia, which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases. Therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Best Breakpoint: End the prompt just before the bone‑marrow biopsy results and the parvovirus B19 PCR, i.e., after the statement that a complete haematological work‑up was commenced. This provides the anemia’s clinical context, negative GI work‑up, reticulocytopenia, and prior therapeutic attempts without revealing the definitive virologic findings.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors ruled out overt GI bleeding (negative CT, endoscopy, colonoscopy, FOBT), rejected pancreas‑allograft rejection as the sole cause (biopsy equivocal, tacrolimus increase ineffective), dismissed CMV duodenitis (negative CMV PCR despite histology, lack of response to ganciclovir), considered TMA (kidney biopsy) but it did not explain the reticulocytopenia, and finally identified parvovirus B19 infection through bone‑marrow inclusions and PCR, leading to successful IVIG therapy.
case_prompt:
A 45‑year‑old Asian man with poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and end‑stage renal disease underwent simultaneous pancreas‑kidney transplantation from a CMV‑seropositive deceased donor. Induction immunosuppression was alemtuzumab; maintenance included tacrolimus, mycophenolate mofetil, and a brief course of prednisolone. Post‑operative recovery was uneventful with primary graft function, and prophylactic valganciclovir was continued for nine months.

Thirteen months post‑transplant he presented with an acute fall in haemoglobin from 138 g/L to 86 g/L without any overt bleeding. Contrast‑enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis, upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, colonoscopy, and a faecal occult blood test were all negative. case_prompt:
A 22‑year‑old Chinese male from Zhejiang province presented to a local community hospital with a 10‑day history of intermittent fever up to 38.7 °C and a 3‑day history of progressive dyspnea and dry cough. Initial therapy with moxifloxacin was stopped after he developed oral thrush and was changed to ambroxol hydrochloride. Because of a history of male sexual partners and recent weight loss, an HIV test was performed and returned positive, prompting referral to the infectious disease department of the First Affiliated Hospital, Zhejiang University.

On admission he continued to have fever, dyspnea, fatigue, cough with a small amount of pale sputum, occasional chest pain, and exertional dyspnea. Vital signs were: temperature 37.4 °C, blood pressure 113/50 mmHg, pulse 115 beats/min, respiratory rate 23 breaths/min, SpO₂ 93 % on room air. Lung examination revealed moist rales bilaterally; no skin rash was noted.

Laboratory studies showed: WBC 7.7 × 10⁹/L (neutrophils 65.7 %), hemoglobin 133 g/L, platelets 365 × 10⁹/L; CRP 8.5 mg/L, ESR 5 mm/h, procalcitonin 0.08 ng/mL. LDH was elevated at 401 U/L (reference 150‑250) and α‑hydroxybutyrate dehydrogenase 326 U/L (reference 72‑182). The serum 1,3‑β‑D‑glucan (G test) was positive at 251.64 pg/mL, whereas galactomannan and cryptococcal capsular antigen tests were negative. CD4⁺ T‑cell count was 16 cells/µL.

Arterial blood gas on 3 L/min nasal O₂ showed pH 7.51, pCO₂ 27 mmHg, pO₂ 98 mmHg, HCO₃⁻ 21.9 mmol/L, lactate 0.8 mmol/L, O₂ saturation 99 %.

Chest CT demonstrated extensive bilateral ground‑glass opacities with multiple thin‑walled cavitary lesions in the left upper lobe. Tests for SARS‑CoV‑2 IgG/IgM and nucleic acid were negative, as were nucleic acid screens for Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Chlamydia pneumoniae, adenovirus, RSV, parainfluenza, influenza A/B. EBV and CMV IgG were positive but IgM negative; quantitative PCR detected CMV DNA at 1.86 × 10⁴ copies/mL. Tuberculosis testing (T‑SPOT.TB, sputum acid‑fast stain, GeneXpert) was negative. Blood, sputum, and urine smears and cultures for bacteria and fungi were negative. A sputum Gomori‑Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) stain for Pneumocystis jirovecii was negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. HIV infection with CD4 = 16 cells/µL creates profound immunosuppression predisposing to opportunistic infections, especially Pneumocystis pneumonia. | "His CD4 count was 16 cells/muL."
2. Diffuse bilateral ground‑glass opacities on chest CT are classic for PCP in AIDS patients. | "CT scan showed extensive ground‑glass opacities in the bilateral lung..."
3. Elevated serum 1,3‑β‑D‑glucan supports a fungal or Pneumocystis infection, while galactomannan and cryptococcal antigen are negative, making aspergillosis and cryptococcosis unlikely. | "The 1,3-beta-D-glucan test (G test) result (251.64 pg/ml) was positive, while galactomannan test (GM test) (0.1 mug/L) and cryptococcus capsular antigen test results were negative."
4. Extensive microbiologic work‑up (negative bacterial cultures, negative viral PCR panel, negative Mycoplasma/Chlamydia PCR) excludes common bacterial and viral pneumonias. | "Nucleic acid detection of common respiratory pathogens... was negative."
5. Tuberculosis is ruled out by negative T‑SPOT.TB, sputum acid‑fast stain, and GeneXpert. | "Mycobacterium tuberculosis (MTB) was negative based on blood test with T‑SPOT.TB as well as acid‑fast staining of sputum smear and GeneXpert."
6. Negative sputum GMS for Pneumocystis reduces sensitivity but does not exclude PCP; bronchoalveolar lavage is more sensitive. | "We also sent the sputum sample to perform Gomori‑Grocott methenamine silver nitrate staining (GMS) for Pneumocystis jirovecii detection and obtained a negative result."
7. CMV DNA detected in blood suggests possible CMV reactivation, but CMV alone rarely produces prominent ground‑glass opacities without other findings; the dominant radiologic pattern and β‑D‑glucan point toward PCP as the primary pathogen. | "The nucleic acid of CMV in the blood was reported at 1.86 × 10⁴ copies/mL by quantitative PCR."
8. Absence of rash, normal eosinophil count, and negative galactomannan make other fungal infections (e.g., aspergillosis) unlikely. | "galactomannan test (GM test) (0.1 mug/L) ... were negative."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case focuses on Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia, which is listed as “pneumocystis” in the 21 SELECTED diseases. No other SELECTED disease is the primary focus.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Stop the narrative immediately before the bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) result confirming P. jirovecii. Include the patient’s transplant background, presenting symptoms, vital signs, initial labs, imaging, and the decision to perform bronchoscopy, but omit the positive BAL finding.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors ruled out SARS‑CoV‑2, tuberculosis, atypical bacterial pneumonia, and early CMV reactivation based on negative PCR/serology and low‑level viremia; they highlighted the characteristic ground‑glass opacities and pneumatoceles on CT, and ultimately confirmed the diagnosis with a positive BAL for P. jirovecii.
case_prompt:
The patient is a 17‑year‑old male with a history of congenital vesicoureteral reflux, chronic kidney disease stage 5, and a deceased‑donor kidney transplant performed in June 2019. His immunosuppressive regimen at the time of presentation consisted of tacrolimus 6 mg PO daily, methylprednisolone 8 mg PO daily, and mycophenolate mofetil 500 mg PO twice daily. He had completed 6 months of CMV prophylaxis with valganciclovir in December 2019 and had previously been treated for CMV viremia (8811 copies/mL) in September 2019.

In late June 2020 he was admitted with sub‑febrile temperature (37.2 °C), dry cough, dyspnea on exertion for one week, and generalized fatigue for more than three weeks. He reported a 4‑kg weight loss (down to 46 kg). Physical examination showed tachycardia (HR 128 bpm), oxygen saturation 89% on room air, and a red, dry maculopapular rash on the upper trunk and neck; lung auscultation was normal. He required 2–3 L/min supplemental O₂ to keep SpO₂ ≥ 92%. Blood pressure was 124/80 mmHg.

Initial laboratory studies revealed eGFR 32 mL/min/1.73 m² (down from baseline), CRP 79.2 mg/L, tacrolimus level 5.7 ng/mL, and normal complete blood count, albumin, liver enzymes, and electrolytes. CMV viremia was low (51 copies/mL). SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR from nasopharyngeal swabs was negative twice. Tuberculosis screening was negative (both TST and IGRA). Serologic tests and PCR for atypical bacterial pathogens were negative. Blood cultures were obtained.

Chest radiograph showed fine bilateral interstitial infiltrates with interstitial edema. Chest CT demonstrated bilateral ground‑glass opacities, basal pneumatoceles, and diffuse centrilobular and peribronchovascular consolidations of varying size.

Given the worsening respiratory status, empiric therapy with IV TMP‑SMX, fluconazole, and ganciclovir was started, MMF was reduced, and a bronchoscopy was performed to obtain bronchoalveolar lavage fluid for definitive diagnosis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. SARS‑CoV‑2 infection considered but excluded by repeated negative PCR. | "PCR tests for SARS‑CoV‑2 from nasopharyngeal swabs were negative twice."
2. Tuberculosis ruled out by negative skin test and interferon‑gamma release assay. | "Tuberculosis was excluded with both negative Tuberculin skin test (TST) and Interferon‑gamma release assay."
3. Atypical bacterial pneumonia excluded by negative serology and PCR. | "Atypical bacterial infections were excluded with negative serological testing and negative nasopharyngeal swab PCR."
4. Early CMV pneumonitis deemed unlikely due to low‑level viremia (51 copies/mL) at admission. | "CMV viremia was present at 51 copies/ml."
5. Fungal skin infection (toenail fungus) considered only for cutaneous lesions; no systemic antifungal evidence. | "Topical antifungal treatment was prescribed for suspected fungal etiology of toenail and skin lesions."
6. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia supported by characteristic CT findings (ground‑glass opacities, pneumatoceles) and confirmed by positive BAL PCR. | "BALF sample tested positive for P. jirovecii."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case centers on a STAT3 gain‑of‑function (GOF) syndrome, which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases; therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.  
2. Breakpoint: Present the clinical presentation, imaging, and initial infectious work‑up up to the chest CT and lung biopsy results, stopping before the description of next‑generation sequencing that identified the STAT3 mutation. This provides sufficient data for students to formulate a differential diagnosis without revealing the genetic etiology.  
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors first entertained congenital interstitial lung disease and severe combined immunodeficiency, then systematically excluded known surfactant‑protein and immunity‑related genes, performed extensive infectious testing (CMV, PCP, TB, HIV, EBV, bacterial cultures), and finally used trio whole‑exome sequencing to uncover a de novo STAT3 GOF mutation, corroborated by functional assays and response to JAK inhibition.
case_prompt: A 1‑year‑old boy, born at term to non‑consanguineous Chinese parents, presented at 4 months of age with eczematous dermatitis, mild cough, and a lump behind the left ear. His respiratory symptoms progressively worsened, leading to respiratory distress and hypoxemia. Bronchoalveolar lavage and blood tests were positive for cytomegalovirus (CMV) DNA. He experienced repeated respiratory infections with sputum cultures growing Acinetobacter baumannii, Klebsiella pneumoniae, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Stenotrophomonas maltophilia, and required intubation twice for respiratory failure. Broad‑spectrum antibiotics temporarily decreased inflammatory markers, but fever recurred during therapy. At 6 months, chest computed tomography showed interstitial lung disease with diffuse ground‑glass opacity. Lung biopsy revealed chronic interstitial lung disease with diffuse thickening of alveolar membranes, hyperplastic type II pneumocytes, and a mild to moderate infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and macrophages; there was no proteinosis or established fibrosis. Microbiological studies of the biopsy (bacterial, fungal, acid‑fast bacillus stains, PCR) and CMV were negative. Bronchoalveolar lavage staining for Pneumocystis jirovecii, blood tests for CMV, Epstein–Barr virus, HIV, β‑glucan, and QuantiFERON‑TB were also negative. Empiric treatment with prednisolone (1.8 mg/kg/day) and hydroxychloroquine (6 mg/kg/day) yielded partial improvement. While chest symptoms stabilized, he developed recurrent diarrhea with leukocytosis, including one episode with stool culture positive for Clostridioides difficile. At 11 months he presented with worsening diarrhea, poor feeding, septic shock, metabolic acidosis, and elevated inflammatory markers, and died of respiratory failure at 1 year of age.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Congenital interstitial lung disease (surfactant‑protein deficiency) was initially considered because of early‑onset diffuse ground‑glass opacities; however, targeted genetic testing for SFTPC, SFTPB, ABCA3, CSF2RA, CSF2RB, NKX2‑1, FOXF1, and SLC7A7 showed no pathogenic variants. | "Genetic tests were done for the known related genes ... but no meaningful mutation was revealed."
2. Severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID) was evaluated given the recurrent infections; whole‑exome sequencing for SCID‑related genes was negative. | "No severe combined immunodeficiency‑related genetic mutation was found."
3. Active CMV infection was identified (BAL and blood CMV DNA positive) and could explain pulmonary deterioration, but CMV PCR on lung tissue was negative, and disease progressed despite antiviral therapy, suggesting CMV was a trigger rather than the sole cause. | "Bronchoalveolar lavage and blood tests for CMV DNA were positive" and "Microbiological investigations of Lung biopsy ... CMV were negative."
4. Bacterial pneumonia caused by Acinetobacter, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas, and Stenotrophomonas accounted for acute exacerbations, yet antibiotics only transiently reduced inflammation and fever recurred, indicating an underlying predisposition. | "Repeated respiratory infections with positive sputum cultures ... Fever recurred while on broad‑spectrum antibiotics."
5. Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia was ruled out by negative BAL staining. | "Bronchoalveolar lavage pneumocystis pneumonia staining ... negative."
6. Tuberculosis was excluded by negative QuantiFERON‑TB and acid‑fast stains. | "QuantiFERON‑TB were negative."
7. HIV infection was excluded by negative serology. | "Blood tests for ... human immunodeficiency virus ... negative."
8. Epstein–Barr virus reactivation was excluded by negative blood PCR. | "Blood tests for ... Epstein‑Barr virus ... negative."
9. Autoimmune interstitial lung disease (e.g., ANCA‑associated vasculitis) was not supported by clinical or histologic findings and no autoantibodies were reported. | (implicit; absence of such data in the report).
10. The final diagnosis of a STAT3 gain‑of‑function syndrome was established after trio next‑generation sequencing identified a de novo heterozygous missense mutation (c.989C>G, p.P330R) not present in population databases. | "A de novo heterozygous missense mutation of the STAT3 gene (c.989C>G, p.P330R) was identified in the patient."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient’s principal illness is Shiga toxin–producing E. coli hemolytic uremic syndrome (STEC‑HUS), which is not on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Although cytomegalovirus (CMV) infection (a SELECTED disease) is mentioned later, it is disclosed only after the breakpoint and would directly reveal the answer, so the mystery to be solved is the out‑of‑scope STEC‑HUS.
2. Best breakpoint: End the prompt just before the sentence that introduces antiviral therapy for CMV‑DNA positivity. At this point the reader has the clinical picture (fever, diarrhea, edema, oliguria, metabolic acidosis, leukocytosis, anemia, thrombocytopenia, AKI), imaging findings, and the positive stool Shiga‑toxin PCR—all sufficient to diagnose STEC‑HUS without any spoiler.
3. Analytic distinctions: The authors first suspected a typical HUS based on the triad of hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure; they then confirmed the STEC etiology by detecting Shiga‑toxin genes in stool. Autoimmune diabetes was ruled out by negative pancreatic autoantibodies and undetectable C‑peptide. CMV infection was identified later via PCR positivity and treated, but it is not required for the primary diagnosis.
case_prompt: A 3‑year‑old girl was brought to the local emergency department on 12 November 2019 with fever of 39 °C, diarrhea, generalized edema, oliguria, and drowsiness. Laboratory evaluation showed metabolic acidosis, leukocytosis, elevated inflammatory markers, anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney failure. Because of the combination of anemia, thrombocytopenia, and renal impairment, a hemolytic‑uremic syndrome (HUS) was suspected, and the child was transferred to the pediatric emergency room of Fondazione IRCCS Ca’ Granda‑Ospedale Maggiore Policlinico. Despite broad‑spectrum antibiotics and supportive care, her condition worsened over the next few days with the development of arterial hypertension. Whole‑body computed tomography demonstrated bilateral pneumonia, bilateral pleural and abdominal effusions, ischemia of the kidneys and pancreas, edema of the colonic wall and the submucosa of the stomach and duodenum, and massive ileal distension. Stool testing for Shiga toxin genes was positive, leading to a diagnosis of STEC‑HUS. Bilateral pleural drains were placed, and the patient received hydration, total parenteral nutrition (75 kcal/kg/day per WHO guidelines), antihypertensive therapy, and supportive care.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Clinical triad of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute renal failure raised suspicion for HUS. | "Suspecting a HUS, the patient was transferred to the pediatric emergency room..."
2. Positive PCR for Shiga‑toxin genes in stool confirmed the STEC etiology of HUS. | "The search for Shiga toxin genes in the stools was positive, which led to a diagnosis of STEC‑HUS."
3. Autoimmune diabetes was excluded by negative glutamic acid decarboxylase and islet cell antibodies and undetectable C‑peptide. | "Glutamic acid decarboxylase and islet cell antibodies were negative and C‑peptide was undetectable."
4. Cytomegalovirus infection was identified later by DNA positivity and treated with antivirals. | "...antiviral therapy for cytomegalovirus (CMV)‑DNA positivity."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient was infected with SARS‑CoV‑2, which is included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list as **covid_19**. The case report provides sufficient clinical and laboratory details (epidemic timing, respiratory symptoms, chest CT, nasopharyngeal swab) to deduce this diagnosis; therefore covid_19 is the primary target diagnosis.
2. Best Breakpoint: End the presentation just after the statement that a chest CT and nasopharyngeal swab were performed. This includes the prodromal respiratory symptoms, severity leading to ICU admission, and the diagnostic work‑up without revealing the positive swab result, allowing the learner to infer a viral respiratory infection (COVID‑19) as the most likely cause.
3. Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished COVID‑19 from a myasthenic crisis (pyridostigmine dose escalation without improvement), from bacterial super‑infection (cultures grew MDR organisms later), from Guillain‑Barré syndrome and other polyneuropathies (normal CSF, negative infectious and autoimmune panels), and from isolated ICU‑acquired weakness (electrophysiology showing critical illness polyneuropathy). These distinctions guided the final attribution of the acute respiratory failure to SARS‑CoV‑2 infection.
case_prompt: A 66‑year‑old man with a past medical history of hypertension and ocular myasthenia gravis, well controlled on pyridostigmine 30 mg three times daily, presented in early December 2020 with fever, cough, myalgia, and progressive dyspnea. His respiratory status deteriorated rapidly, leading to severe respiratory failure that required admission to the intensive care unit. On arrival, a chest computed tomography scan and a nasopharyngeal swab were performed. He was subsequently treated with remdesivir and corticosteroids, required mechanical ventilation, and later a tracheotomy. During his ICU stay he also developed infections with multidrug‑resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa, for which multiple antibiotic regimens were administered. Laboratory testing did not reveal an increase in serum creatine kinase.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. COVID‑19 infection considered due to acute febrile respiratory illness during a pandemic, severe hypoxemic respiratory failure, and need for antiviral therapy | "He underwent chest computer tomography (CT) and nasopharyngeal swab..."
2. Myasthenic crisis entertained because of underlying ocular MG, but lack of response to increased pyridostigmine dosage and unchanged muscle strength suggested otherwise | "Despite this development, pyridostigmine was increased to 60 mg three times daily; the strength remained unchanged."
3. Bacterial pneumonia/sepsis from MDR organisms considered given later culture results, but these pathogens were identified only after the initial respiratory deterioration | "He also developed infections caused by multi‑drug resistant germs, including Klebsiella pneumonia, Acinetobacter baumannii, and Pseudomonas aeruginosa..."
4. Guillain‑Barré syndrome and other inflammatory polyneuropathies ruled out by normal cerebrospinal fluid findings and absence of albumin‑cytologic dissociation | "Pressure, cell count, and protein levels (<45 mg/dl) of the CSF were normal without albumin‑cytologic disassociation."
5. Other viral respiratory infections (influenza, other coronaviruses) considered less likely given the temporal context of the COVID‑19 pandemic and the decision to initiate remdesivir | "He was treated with remdesivir and corticosteroids."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s principal diagnosis is disseminated nocardiosis, which is NOT in the 21 SELECTED diseases list. A cytomegalovirus infection appears later but is not the primary focus. Therefore, the target diagnosis is out‑of‑scope.
2. Breakpoint: Include all data up to the point just before the authors state “The patient was diagnosed with disseminated nocardiosis.” This provides the clinical presentation, imaging, laboratory, and microbiology results that allow the learner to infer the diagnosis without the explicit statement.
3. Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished nocardiosis from bacterial pneumonia, tuberculosis, and other fungal infections by (a) identifying Nocardia farcinica on NGS and sputum/BALF cultures, (b) negative TB assays (Gene Xpert, culture), (c) negative cryptococcal antigen and fungal D‑glucan, and (d) demonstrated CNS lesions compatible with nocardial brain abscesses.
case_prompt:
A 61‑year‑old woman presented to the emergency department on December 27, 2021 with a sudden high fever of 39.4 °C, chills, malaise, cough, and scant white sputum. She had a 15‑year history of rheumatoid arthritis treated with methylprednisolone 2 mg twice daily, and a diagnosis of allergic vasculitis one year prior, for which her steroid dose had been increased to 16 mg twice daily. One month before admission she had lower‑extremity skin ulcers that appeared healed on presentation.

Initial laboratory studies showed leukocytosis (21.5 × 10⁹/L) with neutrophilia (91.1 %), lymphopenia (5.5 %), hemoglobin 118 g/L, platelets 172 × 10⁹/L, CRP 130 mg/L, and procalcitonin 2.45 µg/L; other tests were within normal limits. Chest CT revealed multiple nodular foci with partial cavitations in the lower lobes of both lungs.

She was transferred to the respiratory ward. Vital signs were temperature 36.2 °C, BP 112/60 mmHg, pulse 84 /min, RR 20 /min; she was alert with no systemic symptoms. Repeat chest CT showed small nodules and pulmonary bullae in the right lower lung. Abdominal enhanced CT demonstrated a low‑density focus in the right abdominal wall, small renal stones, a small amount of pelvic fluid, and low‑density nodules adjacent to the upper pole of the right kidney.

Blood next‑generation sequencing performed in the emergency department detected **Nocardia farcinica**. Sputum culture grew **Staphylococcus aureus** and **Nocardia farcinica**; susceptibility testing indicated sensitivity to trimethoprim‑sulfamethoxazole, amikacin, linezolid, and imipenem. Tests for cryptococcal capsular antigen, fungal (1→3)-β‑D‑glucan, T‑cell assay, Gene Xpert for tuberculosis, autoantibodies, and rheumatoid factor were all negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial pneumonia (Staphylococcus aureus) considered because of productive cough and leukocytosis, but Nocardia farcinica was also isolated, and the patient’s lesions were atypical for simple Staph infection. | "Staphylococcus aureus and Nocardia farcinica were found in sputum culture."
2. Tuberculosis entertained given cavitary lung nodules; ruled out by negative Gene Xpert, negative sputum and BALF cultures, and negative CSF TB assays. | "T‑cell and gene Xpert for tuberculosis... were all negative."
3. Cryptococcal meningitis considered because of CNS symptoms; excluded by negative cryptococcal capsular antigen in serum and CSF. | "Cryptococcus neofermans capsule antigen... were all negative."
4. Invasive fungal infection (Aspergillus) contemplated due to nodular lung lesions; initial fungal D‑glucan was negative, and Aspergillus was not isolated until later in the course. | "fungal D‑glucan... were all negative."
5. Non‑nocardial opportunistic infections (e.g., other Nocardia species) deemed less likely because NGS specifically identified **Nocardia farcinica** and cultures repeatedly grew this organism. | "blood next‑generation sequencing (NGS) from the emergency room revealed Nocardia farcinica."
6. Disseminated nocardiosis favored by the combination of (a) identification of Nocardia farcinica in blood NGS, sputum, and later BALF, (b) compatible pulmonary nodules with cavitation, (c) multiple brain lesions on MRI, and (d) appropriate antimicrobial susceptibility. | "The patient was diagnosed with disseminated nocardiosis..." (implicit inference from preceding data)

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient’s primary clinical problem—Stevens‑Johnson syndrome (SJS) with subsequent vanishing bile duct syndrome—is not in the 21 selected diseases list. No other selected disease can be definitively diagnosed from the early presentation. Therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Breakpoint: End the case presentation at the point of admission to our hospital, after documentation of the extensive erythematous‑purpuric rash, mucosal involvement, percentage of body surface area affected, and the initial negative viral/mycoplasma/autoimmune work‑up. Omit any mention of the SJS diagnosis that was already made elsewhere, liver‑function derangements, VBDS, CMV infection, HLH, or treatment details.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished SJS from other acute cutaneous eruptions by (a) the extent of epidermal necrosis (35 % TBSA erythema, 8 % TBSA blistering), (b) involvement of two mucosal sites (conjunctiva, oral), (c) a recent exposure to NSAIDs, and (d) exclusion of infectious (viral panel, Mycoplasma) and autoimmune causes through laboratory testing.
case_prompt: A 42‑year‑old man with a remote history of cured hepatitis C presented with a 9‑day history of fever and sore throat, followed 5 days ago by a rapidly spreading pruritic rash. He had taken mefenamic acid, diclofenac, ibuprofen and acetaminophen over the preceding week for flu‑like symptoms. On examination he was alert, oriented, and hemodynamically stable. His skin showed confluent erythematous‑to‑purpuric macules and patches covering the face, trunk and extremities, with flat erythematous spots on the distal limbs. The total body surface area (TBSA) involved by erythema was estimated at 35 %, with blistering present on 8 % of TBSA. Mucosal involvement included conjunctival injection with ulceration and oral ulcers. Initial investigations included a viral panel, Mycoplasma pneumoniae serology and an autoimmune screen, all of which were negative (Supplementary tables referenced). No new medications had been started within the prior two months aside from the NSAIDs listed. The patient was transferred to our tertiary center for further management.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Stevens‑Johnson syndrome (SJS) was most likely given the abrupt onset of widespread erythematous‑purpuric macules with epidermal detachment, involvement of two mucosal sites, and recent exposure to high‑risk drugs (NSAIDs) | "Generalized confluent erythematous to purpuric macules and patches... with mucosal involvement... after NSAID exposure."
2. Toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN) considered but less likely because the extent of epidermal detachment (<10 % TBSA) fell below the TEN threshold (>30 % TBSA) | "Blistering of 8 % TBSA" indicating limited epidermal loss.
3. Drug‑induced exanthema with secondary infection was ruled out by the absence of systemic signs of bacterial infection and negative cultures, plus the characteristic mucosal lesions which are atypical for simple drug eruptions | "Viral panel, mycoplasma pneumoniae infection and autoimmune survey yielded negative results."
4. Viral exanthem (e.g., measles, EBV) excluded by negative viral panel and lack of classic prodromal enanthem | "Viral panel... yielded negative results."
5. Bullous pemphigoid or other autoimmune blistering diseases deemed unlikely due to the acute onset, extensive mucosal involvement, and negative autoimmune serology | "Autoimmune survey yielded negative results."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case centers on Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency type I (LAD‑I), which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases; therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.  
2. Best Breakpoint: Include presentation, laboratory data, and flow‑cytometry results that reveal markedly decreased CD18 (and CD11b/c) expression, stopping just before the genetic sequencing results are described. This provides sufficient information for a learner to infer LAD‑I without revealing the definitive genetic confirmation.  
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors first noted recurrent omphalitis and extreme leukocytosis, prompting consideration of a leukocyte adhesion defect. Flow cytometry demonstrating near‑absent CD18 on neutrophils narrowed the differential to LAD‑I, and subsequent gene panel sequencing was used to confirm the diagnosis and identify compound heterozygous ITGB2 mutations.
case_prompt: A 5‑month‑old Vietnamese girl was referred for evaluation of recurrent omphalitis (episodes at 6 days, 1 month, and 4 months of age, each treated with IV antibiotics). Her past medical history included a urachal remnant and grade III vesicoureteral reflux. She presented with fever and no obvious focus of infection. Laboratory studies showed marked leukocytosis (WBC 90,970/µL, neutrophils 67,770/µL, lymphocytes 18,190/µL) and elevated C‑reactive protein (15.8 mg/dL). Because recurrent omphalitis and the profound leukocytosis raised suspicion for leukocyte adhesion deficiency (LAD), flow cytometric analysis of peripheral blood neutrophils was performed. CD18 expression was markedly decreased, with only 1.1 % of neutrophils positive for CD18; CD11b and CD11c expression were also reduced.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Recurrent bacterial omphalitis without underlying immunodeficiency – considered due to typical presentation of umbilical infections, but unlikely because the leukocytosis was extreme and neutrophil surface markers were abnormal. | "The history of recurrent omphalitis and the significant leukocytosis suggested LAD as the differential diagnosis."
2. Other primary immunodeficiencies (e.g., severe combined immunodeficiency) – contemplated given the early‑onset infections, yet excluded because flow cytometry revealed a specific deficiency of CD18 (and CD11b/c) rather than a global lymphocyte defect. | "CD18 expression was significantly decreased... CD11b and CD11c expression on the neutrophils also decreased."
3. Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type I – favored because the clinical phenotype (recurrent omphalitis, marked leukocytosis) together with near‑absent CD18 expression matches the hallmark laboratory finding of LAD‑I. | "Based on her clinical phenotype and flow cytometric analysis, LAD‑I was suspected."
final_diagnosis: Leukocyte adhesion deficiency type I -> OUT_OF_SCOPE

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s definitive diagnosis is peripheral T‑cell lymphoma, not otherwise specified (PTCL‑NOS). This disease is not included in the 21 SELECTED diseases list, so it is classified as OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: The presentation should stop immediately after the decision to perform an inguinal lymph‑node excisional biopsy, but before any histopathologic results are disclosed. This provides enough clinical, laboratory, and imaging clues (B symptoms, generalized adenopathy, eosinophilia, abnormal liver enzymes, negative cultures) for the learner to generate a differential that includes a lymphoproliferative disorder without revealing the final pathology.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished between reactive/infectious processes and a true lymphoma by (a) lack of response to broad‑spectrum antibiotics, (b) persistent eosinophilia and systemic B symptoms despite topical steroids, (c) negative bacterial, mycobacterial, and viral tissue studies (EBER‑negative, cultures negative), and (d) definitive immunophenotypic findings on the excisional node biopsy that demonstrated a diffuse CD3⁺ T‑cell infiltrate with loss of CD5, confirming PTCL‑NOS.
case_prompt:
A 68‑year‑old man with a past history of ischemic stroke (2015) and hypertension presented to the emergency department with a 3‑month history of asthenia, anorexia, night sweats (occasionally with perceived fever), and a 2‑week history of intermittent fever. Three days before admission he noted a pruritic maculopapular rash on the trunk and back. He denied immunosuppression or relevant epidemiologic exposures.

Current medications included aspirin, atorvastatin, perindopril, and oral terbinafine 250 mg, which had been stopped after one week because of a “sickness sensation.”

On examination he was febrile (38.9 °C), tachycardic, and had hard, painless, immobile lymphadenopathy in the supraclavicular, axillary, and inguinal regions, with nodes up to 3–4 cm. Laboratory studies showed leukocytosis with neutrophilia, absolute eosinophilia (up to 3.52 × 10⁹/L), elevated cholestatic enzymes (AST 142 U/L, ALT 161 U/L, ALP 166 U/L), total bilirubin 1.92 mg/dL, lactate dehydrogenase 798 IU/L, mild ionized hypercalcemia (1.51 mmol/L), and C‑reactive protein >100 mg/L. Peripheral smear, protein electrophoresis, immunoglobulin levels, free light chains, and serum/urine immunofixation were normal; proteinuria was absent. Serial blood cultures remained negative.

case_prompt:
An 18‑year‑old male presented with a 12‑day history of sudden‑onset, high‑grade, continuous fever with rigors. He had been managed initially as a presumed dengue case based on serology (positive IgM, negative IgG). Eight days after illness onset he developed left‑sided chest pain that worsened when lying flat and improved on leaning forward. He denied dysuria, diarrhoea, productive cough, or headache. Past medical history was notable for a patent ductus arteriosus (PDA). He reported contact with his grandfather, who had active tuberculosis.

On admission his blood pressure was 140/80 mm Hg, pulse 140 bpm, temperature 101 °F, respiratory rate 20/min, and oxygen saturation 90% on room air. General examination showed pallor; there were no puncture marks, jugular venous distension, or engorged neck veins. Cardiac examination revealed a machinery murmur at the left second intercostal space; no pericardial rub was heard. Lung auscultation was normal except for decreased air entry at the left base. The rest of the systemic examination was unremarkable.

Electrocardiogram demonstrated sinus tachycardia with concave ST‑segment elevation and PR depression in leads I, II, aVL, V2, with reciprocal ST depression and PR elevation in aVR. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 12.1 g/dL, leukocytosis 17 × 10⁹/L, and ESR 60 mm/h. Blood cultures grew methicillin‑resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Dengue IgM remained positive; tuberculosis immunochromatographic test was negative. Chest radiograph showed an increased cardiothoracic ratio, prominent left pulmonary artery markings, and bilateral irregular opacities. Two‑dimensional echocardiography revealed circumferential pericardial effusion and a small PDA with normal left ventricular function.

Twelve hours after admission the patient developed acute shortness of breath, worsening chest pain, blood pressure 90/60 mm Hg, and heart rate 150 bpm, raising concern for impending cardiac tamponade. A pericardial window and PDA ligation were planned. Infective endocarditis associated with the PDA was considered because of one major criterion (positive blood culture) and three minor criteria (fever >38 °C, predisposing cardiac lesion, and septic pulmonary emboli on CT). The CT chest demonstrated infiltrates in the lung fields consistent with septic emboli.

Dengue fever considered initially due to positive IgM serology but excluded because bacteremia with MRSA and presence of murmur, PDA, and septic emboli are atypical for dengue; "The patient was initially managed as a presumed case of dengue fever based on serology: positive Ig M antibody and negative Ig G antibody."

Infective endocarditis favored as the unifying diagnosis because it fulfills Duke’s criteria (one major: positive blood culture; three minor: fever, predisposing cardiac lesion, septic emboli) and explains the pericardial effusion and pulmonary findings; "Infective endocarditis in association with PDA was considered a possibility due to the presence of one major criterion and three minor criteria: the Duke's criteria."

case_prompt: A 38‑year‑old woman from Sullana, Piura, Peru, previously healthy, was diagnosed with dengue (positive IgM ELISA) and received outpatient symptomatic care. Four weeks later she developed intense pain in the anterior cervical region radiating to the mandible and auricular area, along with swelling of that region, general malaise, odynophagia, dysphagia, palpitations, and limb tremor. Cervical ultrasound revealed a heterogeneous thyroid gland and, in the left lobe, a solid, hypoechogenic nodule with irregular margins measuring 27 × 15 mm, classified as ACR‑TIRADS 4. The patient experienced marked cervical pain when the transducer contacted the neck. On admission she had palpitations and resting tremor suggestive of thyrotoxicosis. Laboratory tests showed TSH 0.043 IUI/mL, elevated free T4 and free T3, negative anti‑thyroperoxidase and anti‑thyroglobulin antibodies, and elevated serum thyroglobulin. case_prompt:
A 52‑year‑old man presented to the emergency department after a sudden loss of consciousness lasting one hour. The day before, he had experienced a severe headache with nausea and more than five episodes of vomiting. His family denied seizures, limb weakness, facial droop, or prior head trauma. His past medical history was significant for hypertension (untreated) and hospitalization five days earlier for dengue hemorrhagic fever, during which laboratory testing showed thrombocytopenia (30,000/µL) and a positive IgM dengue antibody; he was discharged on day 4.

On arrival, he was unresponsive, febrile (38.6 °C), and hypertensive (160/90 mm Hg). Pulse was 102/min, respiratory rate 24/min, and SpO₂ 97 % on room air. Neurologic examination revealed a Glasgow Coma Scale of 3/15, no meningeal irritation, and anisocoric pupils (right 6 mm, left 2 mm) with absent light reflexes. Laboratory tests showed normal glucose (136 mg/dL), persistent thrombocytopenia (74 × 10³/µL), hemoglobin 14.3 g/dL, hematocrit 41 %, normal leukocyte count, coagulation profile, and renal function.

A chest X‑ray demonstrated mild cardiomegaly. Non‑contrast CT of the head revealed a wide, hyperdense lesion in the right frontotemporoparietal region extending to the falx cerebri, with a hypodense transition suggestive of a subacute subdural hematoma. Midline shift, a narrowed left ventricle, and surrounding cerebral edema were also noted.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Subdural hematoma suggested by CT morphology – “CT scan showed a wide, hyperdense lesion… with a hypodense transition suggestive of a subacute SDH” |
2. Intracerebral hemorrhage considered less likely because the lesion is extra‑axial and conforms to the falx, not typical of parenchymal bleed – “hyperdense lesion… extending to the falc cerebri” |
3. Meningitis/encephalitis excluded by lack of meningeal signs – “without signs of meningeal irritation” |
4. Metabolic encephalopathy deemed unlikely given focal mass effect and anisocoric pupils – “midline shift… cerebral edema… anisocoric pupils with a negative light reflex” |
5. Infectious process (bacterial meningitis) considered, prompting empiric ceftriaxone, but imaging did not support meningeal enhancement – “antibiotics, ceftriaxone injection… were also given” |

case_prompt: A 28‑year‑old woman was hospitalized for acute‑onset high fever, myalgia, arthralgia and ocular pain. Detailed history‑taking, hematological and serological investigations were performed. Seven days later, during the convalescent phase, she noticed blurring of the inferior visual field in the right eye and presented two weeks after the ocular symptoms began. Best‑corrected visual acuity was 20/20 bilaterally. Slit‑lamp examination showed an unremarkable anterior segment in both eyes, with no anterior vitreous cells or flare. Fundus examination of the right eye revealed a patchy area of partially faded retinal whitening in the superotemporal quadrant of the macula, encroaching into the fovea, accompanied by attenuation and sclerosis of the macular division of the superotemporal branch retinal artery. The left fundus showed a single cotton‑wool spot near the inferotemporal arcade. Mid‑phase fluorescein angiogram of the right eye demonstrated narrowing of the affected arterial segment, blocked background fluorescence in the whitening area, delayed arteriovenous transit, and late‑phase staining and leakage of the occluded artery. Kinetic central field testing with Bjerrum’s screen displayed an inferonasal field defect corresponding to the arterial occlusion. A detailed cardiac and carotid evaluation—including carotid Doppler study and echocardiography—was unremarkable. The patient was followed for three months; visual acuity remained 20/20 in both eyes, but the inferior field defect persisted in the right eye.

1. Dengue fever as the etiologic agent for the febrile illness and subsequent retinal vascular event | “Detailed history‑taking, hematological and serological investigations established the diagnosis of classic dengue fever (a positive IgM antibody titer)”.
2. Leptospirosis excluded as a mimic of the acute febrile syndrome | “ruled out mimicking infections like leptospirosis…”.

5. Syphilis excluded as a mimic of the acute febrile syndrome | “…syphilis…”.
6. Collagen vascular diseases excluded as alternative causes of ocular inflammation | “…as well as collagen vascular diseases”.
7. Embolic or atherothrombotic source of branch retinal artery occlusion excluded by normal systemic vascular work‑up | “cardiac and carotid evaluation … was unremarkable”.

case_prompt:
A 19‑year‑old male with no known comorbidities presented to an outside hospital after two weeks of high‑grade fever and a productive cough with scant sputum. Physical examination revealed decreased air entry on the right side with a stony‑dull percussion note. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and metabolic panel, but an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 40 mm/hour. Chest radiography demonstrated blunting of the right costo‑phrenic angle consistent with a right‑sided pleural effusion. Thoracentesis yielded an exudative, lymphocytic‑predominant pleural fluid, leading to a clinical diagnosis of tuberculous pleuritis and initiation of four‑drug antituberculous therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol).

The regimen required several modifications because of adverse drug reactions: pyrazinamide caused hyperuricemia, ofloxacin produced severe gastrointestinal symptoms, streptomycin induced vertiginous otologic toxicity, and ethambutol caused bilateral optic neuritis confirmed by visual evoked potentials. While on the modified regimen, the patient experienced a generalized tonic‑clonic seizure; brain MRI showed right frontal, temporal, parietal, and cerebellar parenchymal lesions, and phenytoin was started.

Two months into therapy, a repeat chest x‑ray showed bilateral pleural effusions. A second thoracentesis again revealed an exudative, lymphocytic‑predominant fluid with a markedly elevated adenosine deaminase level (135.2 U/L). Bronchoalveolar lavage smear was negative for acid‑fast bacilli, and transbronchial lung biopsy showed multiple ill‑defined epithelioid granulomas with inflammatory infiltrates.

The patient was referred with persistent moderate‑to‑high‑grade fever, cough, worsening bilateral pleural effusions, and new epistaxis. Examination disclosed a febrile, tachycardic, cachectic young man with a florid petechial rash over the chest and abdomen, decreased bilateral chest expansion, hepatosplenomegaly, hemoglobin 7.6 g/dL, platelet count 29 000/µL, mildly elevated AST (87 U/L) and ALT (68 U/L), and markedly raised alkaline phosphatase (1743 U/L). Coagulation studies were normal. Investigations to exclude other causes of fever were unrevealing: urinalysis, blood and urine cultures, peripheral smear for malaria, dengue serology, Widal test, antistreptolysin O titers, and echocardiography were all negative.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Tuberculous pleural effusion suggested by exudative, lymphocytic fluid with high ADA | "A diagnostic thoracentesis was performed that revealed an exudative, lymphocytic‑predominant pleural fluid... repeat ... high adenosine deaminase (ADA) content of 135.2 (normal <40)".
2. Persistent fever despite adequate ATT raised concern for drug‑resistant or disseminated TB vs. drug toxicity | "Patient had significant side effects to many drugs... While on modified ATT, the patient had a generalized tonic‑clonic seizure."
3. Brain MRI lesions could represent tuberculomas rather than other intracranial pathology | "Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the brain done revealed right frontal, temporal, parietal, and cerebellar parenchymal lesions."
4. Negative microbiologic studies for other infections (malaria, dengue, bacterial sepsis) argued against alternative infectious etiologies | "Other laboratory investigations done to rule out other causes of persistent fever... negative blood, and urine cultures, no malaria parasite on peripheral smear, negative dengue serologies..."
5. Histopathology showing necrotizing epithelioid granulomas supported TB over malignancy or other granulomatous diseases | "Bone biopsy revealed multiple necrotizing epithelioid cell granulomas with areas of diffuse necrosis consistent with disseminated tuberculosis."
6. Presence of hepatosplenomegaly, miliary‑type pulmonary nodules (later described) and necrotic mediastinal nodes are classic for disseminated TB, distinguishing it from isolated pleural disease | (Implied from radiologic description preceding the final diagnosis).
7. Drug‑induced immune thrombocytopenia considered but platelet count improved markedly after corticosteroids, indicating immune‑mediated process secondary to TB rather than drug toxicity alone | "The platelet count showed rapid recovery following initiation of immunomodulatory therapy, with a platelet count of 285 000/cu.mm after a week of prednisone."

case_prompt: A 25‑year‑old male businessman from Srinagar returned from a week‑long trip to Delhi in October 2012. Two days after returning he developed fever, chills, myalgias, and headache, for which he took paracetamol. He subsequently experienced worsening headache and a high‑grade fever of 102 °F, prompting admission. Physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory studies showed a normal hemogram except for thrombocytopenia (86 000/mm³); renal and liver function tests, urinalysis, chest X‑ray, and abdominal ultrasound were within normal limits. Because Delhi was experiencing a dengue outbreak and the platelet count was low, an IgM ELISA for dengue virus was performed and returned positive, leading to a provisional diagnosis of dengue fever and initiation of supportive therapy. Despite this, the patient continued to have fever spikes and chills. Given Delhi’s endemicity for malaria, a rapid malaria antigen test (pLDH/HRP2) and thick and thin peripheral blood smears were ordered.

Dengue fever considered due to recent travel to an area with a known outbreak and thrombocytopenia | "Since the patient had visited Delhi during an outbreak of dengue and was found to have a low platelet count, a viral serology test using IgM ELISA for dengue virus was carried out that turned out to be positive."

case_prompt:
A 38‑year‑old male Guatemalan soldier presented on June 29, 2012, to the Military Hospital for evaluation of suspected malaria. Three months earlier he had returned from a 9‑month deployment in the Democratic Republic of Congo, with additional short stays in Uganda and Kenya. During the mission he used an untreated bed net and received mefloquine prophylaxis (250 mg base/week) but admitted to skipping doses while in Uganda and Kenya. Upon return to Guatemala, all personnel were screened for malaria by microscopy and PCR, which were negative.

Two months after returning, he traveled to a coastal region of southern Guatemala where malaria is endemic. He subsequently developed fatigue and fever and was clinically diagnosed with malaria by a private physician, receiving chloroquine injections. He improved, returned to duty, but three weeks later presented again with fever and fatigue. Microscopy at the regional malaria program reported a Plasmodium vivax infection, and he was transferred to the Military Medical Center.

At admission, a thin blood film was read as P. vivax, but the hospital microbiologist expressed concerns about the morphology of some observed parasites. Laboratory studies showed thrombocytopenia (71 × 10³/µL) and anemia (hemoglobin 12 g/dL). A rapid dengue diagnostic assay was positive for a current or recent infection. Other laboratory tests were within normal limits.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Initial consideration of Plasmodium vivax malaria based on endemicity and clinical presentation | "A thin blood film identified P. vivax, although concerns about the morphology of some of the observed parasites were raised by the hospital microbiologist."
2. Dengue infection as a concurrent or alternative diagnosis because of positive rapid test and thrombocytopenia | "A rapid dengue diagnostic assay showed a current or recent infection."
3. Possibility of non‑indigenous malaria species (e.g., P. ovale) given travel to African endemic areas and morphological doubts | "Based on the travel history of the patient and the doubts arisen as to its species identity, molecular testing was conducted to confirm the Plasmodium species."
4. Consideration of other malaria species (P. malariae) as part of broader differential in imported cases, though not initially identified | "This report highlights the need to consider P. ovale as a cause of imported malaria and to include its detection, as well as P. malariae, in imported malaria screening programs."

case_prompt: A 22‑year‑old male of Caribbean descent presented with several weeks of diminished vision, ocular pain, and photosensitivity in the right eye. case_prompt: A 19‑year‑old Nigerian college student presented to the emergency department with a 4‑day history of fever, chills, rigors, and generalized body aches. He had returned from a 10‑day visit to Nigeria five days before symptom onset. On examination his temperature was 39.8 °C, pulse 126 beats/min, and blood pressure 128/87 mm Hg; no other significant physical findings were noted. A BinaxNOW malaria rapid test produced a T2 line but no T1 line, indicating a non‑falciparum species (suggestive of vivax, malariae or ovale). Microscopy of thick and thin blood films revealed malaria parasites with an estimated parasitaemia of 0.27 %, interpreted as consistent with P. ovale or P. vivax.

7. Microscopy confirmed the presence of malaria parasites with low parasitaemia, supporting a diagnosis of malaria caused by a non‑falciparum species (P. ovale or P. vivax). | "Microscopy on thick and thin blood films detected the presence of malaria parasites suggesting P. ovale or P. vivax ... with 0.27 % parasitaemia."
