case_prompt:
A 55‑year‑old woman from Mugu, a visceral leishmaniasis‑endemic district in western Nepal, presented to the outpatient department with a 2‑year history of multiple, progressively enlarging, painless nodular lesions confined to her tongue. She reported mild dysphagia but denied fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Examination revealed several well‑circumscribed, erythematous, round‑to‑oval nodules, 1–2 cm in diameter, on the dorsal and lateral tongue surfaces; the nodules were smooth, non‑ulcerated, and not bleeding. No hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy, or cutaneous lesions elsewhere were detected. Differential diagnoses considered initially included infectious diseases such as Hansen’s disease and tuberculosis, as well as mucosal neuromas, sarcoidosis, amyloidosis, and mycosis fungoides.

An incisional biopsy of a tongue lesion showed hyperplastic stratified squamous epithelium overlying a dense dermal infiltrate with fibrotic stroma and striated muscle fibers. The submucosa contained a dense infiltrate of lymphocytes, plasma cells, and histiocytes with multiple well‑formed epithelioid granulomas, involving the striated muscle. No Leishman‑Donovan bodies were seen on hematoxylin‑eosin or Giemsa stains. A slit‑skin smear for Giemsa staining could not be obtained because of the tongue’s rich vascularity, so tissue biopsy was prioritized.

Despite the absence of a prior visceral leishmaniasis diagnosis, leishmaniasis remained a consideration based on endemicity and the granulomatous histology. rK‑39 serology was positive, although its sensitivity in mucosal PKDL is limited. Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) targeting L. donovani DNA was performed. Slit‑skin smear and special stains were negative for acid‑fast bacilli and Congo red. HIV serology was negative. No histologic or clinical features suggested mycosis fungoides.

Slit‑skin smear and special stains were negative for acid‑fast bacilli..."
2. Tuberculosis considered given granulomatous inflammation; excluded by negative acid‑fast stains, absence of systemic TB signs, and lack of Mycobacterium on histology. | "The initial differential diagnosis was broad and included... tuberculosis... Slit‑skin smear and special stains were negative for acid‑fast bacilli..."
3. Mucosal neuromas considered due to nodular tongue lesions; excluded by histology showing granulomatous inflammation rather than proliferative neural tissue. | "The initial differential diagnosis was broad and included... mucosal neuromas... Although rK‑39 serology was positive, its limited sensitivity in mucosal PKDL necessitated molecular confirmation."

case_prompt: A middle‑aged male farmer presented with a recurrent trophic ulcer over the forefoot that had persisted for four years. He had completed a course of multi‑drug therapy ten years earlier and had been free of active disease. Previous management at multiple centres—including walking cast, regular dressings, skin grafting, and fillet flaps from the great and second toes—had ultimately failed, and the ulcer recurred. On examination he had a large trophic ulcer involving the first, second, and third metatarsal‑head region. X‑ray demonstrated characteristic pencilling and tapering of the distal end of the metatarsal. Clinical assessment and handheld Doppler showed good flow in the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial arteries. Sensation was reduced over the entire sole and foot. Debridement removed necrotic tissue and osteomyelitic bone. The resultant defect measured 7 cm × 6 cm, precluding use of a local flap. A 13‑cm‑long pedicle was required; therefore, a radial artery forearm flap from the right non‑dominant forearm was planned. The flap was raised under tourniquet control, with end‑to‑side anastomosis of the radial artery to the dorsalis pedis and end‑to‑end anastomosis of the cephalic vein to the venae comitantes; venous anastomosis was performed before the arterial anastomosis, and the donor site was split‑skin grafted.

1. Prior multi‑drug therapy suggests a history of a chronic infectious disease known to cause peripheral neuropathy and bone changes | "He had completed multi‑drug therapy ten years back and was free of active disease."

4. Radiographic “pencilling” of the distal metatarsal is a classic osseous manifestation of the underlying disease | "There was a characteristic pencilling and tapering of the distal end of the metacarpal on X‑ray."

case_prompt:

Laboratory studies showed low hemoglobin, elevated white blood cell count, low platelets, raised liver enzymes, and deranged renal function; hepatitis B surface antigen and hepatitis C antibody were non‑reactive. He received intravenous artesunate (3 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24 h), IV paracetamol, supportive therapy, and a transfusion of 366 mL whole blood.

On day 2 he developed high fever (40.1 °C) with chills and rigors, decreased consciousness (Blantyre coma score 4/5), and dyspnea (respiratory rate 30/min). Chest exam revealed bilateral vesicular breath sounds with adequate air entry; oxygen saturation was 99 % on 6 L/min intranasal oxygen. A nasopharyngeal swab was obtained for COVID‑19 testing. By day 3, post‑transfusion labs showed improvement in hemoglobin and liver enzymes; urine analysis revealed trace leukocytes, blood +, and protein +. 

On day 5 cefpodoxime suspension 100 mg twice daily was started for 5 days while other treatments continued. Repeat labs showed no malaria parasites and a drop of ~1 g/dL in hemoglobin with normalization of platelets. A 9‑month‑old female was brought with a 2‑week history of cough, high‑grade continuous fever, and progressive poor weight gain since birth despite adequate feeding. One week prior she developed fast breathing and, for the preceding 24 hours, was unable to suckle. Review of systems noted orthopnea, easy fatigability, and excessive sweating; there was no cyanosis, edema, or seizures. She had previously received a blood transfusion at another hospital with no improvement.

On examination the infant was severely pale and in marked respiratory distress with subcostal and intercostal retractions, nasal flaring, and an oxygen saturation of 85 % on room air. She was dysmorphic with upward‑slanting palpebral fissures, low‑set ears, and a flattened nasal bridge. Weight was 6 kg (44 % of expected, > ‑3 Z‑score) and height 72 cm (0.8 Z‑score). Respiratory rate was 60 /min with widespread crepitations. Cardiac examination revealed a displaced apex, tachycardia (160 bpm), a grade 3/6 continuous systolic murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border radiating to the axilla, and an active precordium. Abdominal exam showed a reducible umbilical hernia and tender hepatomegaly (liver 4 cm below the right costal margin).

Initial laboratory studies demonstrated leukocytosis (WBC 22.7 × 10⁹/L), anemia (PCV 28 %), hypokalemia (2.4 mmol/L), and hypocalcemia (non‑ionic calcium 1.09 mmol/L). HIV serology was negative. A peripheral smear was positive for malaria parasites. Chest radiograph showed diffuse perihilar mottled and fluffy opacities involving all lung zones bilaterally, cardiomegaly with a cardiothoracic ratio of 61 %, and splaying of the carina suggestive of cardiogenic pulmonary edema. ECG revealed sinus tachycardia, right atrial enlargement, right‑ventricular hypertrophy, and right‑axis deviation. Echocardiography identified a 0.4 cm patent ductus arteriosus with left‑to‑right shunt at 74 mmHg.

She received parenteral antibiotics, diuretics, supplemental oxygen, nutritional rehabilitation, vitamin D, antimalarial therapy, and hematinics, and was discharged for planned PDA ligation, which was performed six months later with successful closure.

One month post‑surgery she developed cough and, although weight improved to 94 % of expected, she had localized rhonchi in the left upper lung zone. She was treated for early pneumonia and later for two additional uncomplicated outpatient pneumonias. Over the next three months the cough worsened, fever recurred, and weight loss re‑emerged. On re‑presentation she was tachypneic with bilateral coarse crepitations, tachycardic with a gallop rhythm, and again had tender hepatomegaly. She was admitted for severe bronchopneumonia in heart failure “to rule out PTB”. A repeat chest X‑ray demonstrated bilateral perihilar mottled opacity.

3. Malaria infection identified as a possible cause of fever and anemia. | "The malaria parasite was positive."

A diagnosis of PTB was made and she was commenced on anti‑tuberculosis drugs with a good response."

case_prompt:
A 60‑year‑old man with asthma, rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate, and hypertension returned to the United States from a trip to Nigeria. One day after return he developed generalized weakness, intermittent fevers, nausea, vomiting, and mild abdominal pain. Two days before leaving Nigeria he had begun having intermittent fevers and was diagnosed with a malarial infection; he was started on artemether‑lumefantrine but discontinued the regimen within two days because symptoms did not improve. He denied use of herbal supplements.

He presented to the emergency department three days after symptom onset. He was hemodynamically stable and the physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory testing showed:
- Complete blood count, Plasmodium species antigen, Plasmodium falciparum antigen, and thick/thin blood smears: all negative.
- Respiratory infection PCR panel and hepatitis viral antigen/antibody panel: negative.
- AST 1,331 U/L (normal 10–50) and ALT 259 U/L (normal 5–50).
- Creatinine 2.57 mg/dL and BUN 29 mg/dL (normal BUN 8–23) indicating intrinsic AKI.
- Protein/creatinine ratio 74 mg/g (normal 0–30).

Abdominal ultrasound and CT showed no intra‑abdominal pathology. Chest X‑ray and abdominal CT revealed focal interstitial thickening and ground‑glass infiltrates in the left lower lung lobe, consistent with pneumonia.

The patient was admitted, started on atovaquone‑proguanil for possible malaria, and the following day received azithromycin and ceftriaxone for suspected pulmonary infection along with intravenous fluids for AKI. On hospital day 3 (two days after treatment initiation) his CK rose above 19,000 U/L, indicating rhabdomyolysis, and his liver enzymes worsened, prompting aggressive intravenous hydration.

Because of the worsening renal function and proteinuria, a percutaneous renal needle biopsy was performed. (Biopsy findings are reported in the article but are not included here.)

1. Malaria as the primary etiology – The patient had recent travel to a malaria‑endemic region, a prior diagnosis of malaria, incomplete antimalarial therapy, persistent fever, hepatic dysfunction, AKI, and rhabdomyolysis, all of which are recognized complications of severe malaria. | "Two days prior to leaving Nigeria, he noted the onset of intermittent fevers, was diagnosed with malarial infection, and was subsequently started on artemether‑lumefantrine… he discontinued his artemether‑lumefantrine course within the first two days of symptom onset."
2. Negative malaria diagnostics do not exclude infection – Initial rapid antigen tests and microscopy were negative, but the authors note that these results could reflect suppression of parasitemia after partial treatment. | "Complete blood counts, Plasmodium species antigen blood tests, Plasmodium falciparum antigen blood tests, light microscopy of thick and thin blood smears… were all unremarkable. These results indicated possible but unconfirmed suppression of malarial infection by the time of testing."
3. Pulmonary infection considered but not supported – Imaging showed infiltrates, yet respiratory PCR panel was negative and no focal infectious source was identified, making bacterial pneumonia less likely. | "Chest X‑ray revealed focal interstitial thickening and ground‑glass infiltrates… Respiratory infection PCR panel… were all unremarkable."
4. Viral hepatitis ruled out – Hepatitis viral antigen and antibody panels were negative despite marked transaminase elevation, arguing against viral hepatitis as the cause of liver injury. | "Hepatitis viral antigen and antibody panel were all unremarkable."
5. Drug‑induced toxicity considered – Azithromycin and ceftriaxone were started after admission, but the temporal sequence (CK elevation and AKI preceded antimicrobial therapy) makes drug toxicity unlikely. | "On the third day of the admission… he was found to have rhabdomyolysis… prompting aggressive hydration."
6. Rhabdomyolysis as a mechanism – Extremely high CK (>19,000 U/L) and subsequent renal biopsy showing myoglobin casts confirmed rhabdomyolysis, which can be precipitated by severe malaria. | "He was found to have rhabdomyolysis with creatine kinase (CK) level above 19,000 U/L… many tubular granular eosinophilic casts… which stained positively for myoglobin."
7. Acute kidney injury secondary to myoglobin casts – The biopsy demonstrated acute tubular injury with myoglobin casts, linking the AKI to rhabdomyolysis rather than primary glomerular disease. | "Evidence of acute tubular injury… there were many tubular granular eosinophilic casts… stained positively for myoglobin."

A 42‑year‑old single female civil servant with no past medical history presented to an outpatient clinic with a 2‑week history of occasional colicky abdominal pain localized to the right flank, non‑radiating, without clear aggravating or relieving factors. On exam she was mildly pallorous with mild epigastric tenderness; vital signs were stable and weight was 77 kg. Three weeks later she returned with worsening generalized abdominal pain, frequent loose stools, vomiting, loss of appetite, and unintentional weight loss. Laboratory studies showed serum potassium 3.22 mmol/L (reference 3.5‑5.1), haematocrit 24 % (reference 35‑59 %), and a non‑reactive serology test. The patient’s condition continued to decline with persistent vomiting, further weight loss (total loss of 7 kg since surgery), and mild distension with tenderness in the right upper abdomen; no organomegaly was noted.

A contrast‑enhanced abdominal CT scan performed three days after readmission demonstrated dilated bowel loops with mottled hypodensities in the caecum, ascending colon, and transverse colon, consistent with fecal impaction. He received one dose each of doxycycline, atovaquone/proguanil, and artemether/lumefantrine but vomited within an hour. He was transferred to a tertiary ICU for exchange transfusion and started on intravenous artesunate (2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12, 24, and 48 h) followed by a 3‑day oral atovaquone/proguanil course. Chest radiograph was normal, blood cultures were negative, and hemoglobin on admission was 125 g/L. Parasitemia became undetectable within 36 h, and he was discharged after 5 days.  

Four days after discharge, he returned with fever and “merlot‑colored” urine beginning 2 days after discharge. On re‑admission he was jaundiced. Labs showed bilirubin 89 µmol/L, LDH 1,976 U/L (ref 120‑240), hemoglobin 81 g/L, and marked hemoglobinuria; repeat thick and thin smears were negative for *Plasmodium*. Over the next days he required eight red‑cell transfusions to keep hemoglobin >75 g/L. Hemolysis persisted with a nadir hemoglobin of 68 g/L, LDH peak 3,429 U/L, and low haptoglobin (<0.12 g/L). Glucose‑6‑phosphate dehydrogenase was normal. Hemolysis resolved spontaneously 10 days after onset. At 6‑week follow‑up he was asymptomatic with hemoglobin 135 g/L. Testing did not reveal red‑cell alloantibodies, and serology was positive for schistosomiasis, strongyloidiasis, and Q‑fever—considered past infections and not contributory.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction considered but excluded because “pre‑ and post‑transfusion and follow‑up testing did not show evidence of red blood cell alloantibodies, making the possibility of a delayed hemolytic transfusion reaction unlikely.”  
2. G6PD deficiency evaluated and ruled out as “his glucose‑6‑phosphate dehydrogenase level was within reference range.”  
3. Ongoing malaria infection was excluded by negative blood smears: “multiple thick and thin blood smears were negative for *Plasmodium* spp.” and parasitemia had been undetectable within 36 h of the first admission.  
4. Prior parasitic/zoonotic infections (schistosomiasis, strongyloidiasis, Q‑fever) were deemed irrelevant: “Serologic tests showed that he was also positive for causative organisms… These diagnoses were consistent with past infections and were not considered to be contributory to the current severe hemolytic event.”  
5. Hemolysis due to other antimalarial agents (doxycycline, atovaquone/proguanil, artemether/lumefantrine) was deemed unlikely because “severe intravascular hemolysis has rarely been reported in relationship to these agents.”  
6. Drug‑induced immune hemolysis was considered but not substantiated: “We cannot exclude a potential role for drug‑induced immune hemolysis,” yet no alloantibodies or other immunologic markers were identified.

case_prompt:
An 8‑year‑old Nigerian boy was brought to the emergency department 50 minutes after receiving multiple bee stings on the head. He reported passing “bloody urine” at the scene. He had been taken first to a private clinic where he received intravenous 5 % dextrose saline, intravenous Ampiclox, intravenous hydrocortisone, and intramuscular diclofenac, and was then referred for further care.

His past medical history was notable for sickle cell anaemia diagnosed at 8 months of age; he had been stable for more than one year before this episode.

On arrival he was vomiting and had watery, non‑bloody diarrhoea. Examination showed extensive swelling of the head and face, moderate pallor, a temperature of 37.6 °C, mild jaundice, and blood pressure of 90/60 mm Hg. The remainder of the vital signs were unremarkable. A 3‑cm splenomegaly was palpable.

Initial laboratory investigations revealed: packed cell volume 20 %; white‑blood‑cell count 28 700/mm³ with a normal differential; peripheral blood film with poikilocytosis and anisocytosis consistent with haemolysis; platelet count 84 000/mm³. Serum electrolytes, urea and creatinine were within normal limits. A rapid malaria parasite test was positive. Urinalysis dipstick showed blood (++++) with otherwise normal parameters.

He was transfused with one unit of fresh whole blood and started on intravenous antibiotics, intravenous antihistamines, intravenous antimalarial therapy, zinc, and acetaminophen tablets. Hydrocortisone was discontinued. Visible stingers were scraped from the scalp.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Acute hemolytic crisis secondary to sickle cell disease precipitated by bee stings – The authors linked the rapid drop in packed cell volume and smear evidence of hemolysis to the recent bee sting exposure in a known sickle‑cell patient. | “His laboratory investigations revealed a packed cell volume of 20 %…Peripheral blood film showed evidence of haemolysis…He is a known sickle cell anaemia patient…multiple bee stings on the head…He developed incoherent speech and became delirious within 24 hours, and died after 36 hours” (implying the hemolytic cascade).
2. Malaria infection as a potential cause of haemolysis – A positive malaria parasite test was noted, which can cause hemolysis, but the authors considered it insufficient to explain the acute severity in the context of the bee sting trigger. | “Malaria parasite test was positive (+).” (authors later emphasise the temporal relation to bee stings).
3. Anaphylactic reaction to bee venom – The initial management with antihistamines and hydrocortisone reflects concern for anaphylaxis, yet the predominant laboratory picture of hemolysis rather than isolated allergic manifestations led the authors to favour hemolysis over pure anaphylaxis. | “He received …hydrocortisone and intramuscular diclofenac…IV antihistamines…Visible stingers were scrapped off…” (suggesting allergy was considered but not the primary diagnosis).
4. Bacterial sepsis – Empiric intravenous antibiotics were started, indicating sepsis was a differential; however, the marked hemolysis, low PCV, and normal differential count argued against a primary septic picture. | “IV antibiotics…IV antimalarial…He was transfused…” (use of antibiotics reflects sepsis concern, later ruled out by hemolysis findings).
5. Drug‑induced hemolysis (e.g., from Ampiclox) – Administration of antibiotics raised the possibility of drug‑related hemolysis, but the rapid onset after bee stings and the sickle‑cell background made this less likely. | “IV Ampiclox…IV hydrocortisone” (drug exposure acknowledged but not implicated as primary cause).
final_diagnosis: Acute hemolytic crisis in sickle cell disease -> OUT_OF_SCOPE

case_prompt: A 29‑year‑old woman with known chronic kidney disease presented with a four‑month history of intermittent high‑grade fever and poor appetite. She denied dysuria, cough, or abdominal pain. Examination revealed left‑sided axillary lymphadenopathy; there was no hepatosplenomegaly, breast or neurological abnormality. Admission labs showed creatinine 6.9 mg/dL (eGFR 7 mL/min/1.73 m²), hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL, leukocytes 5,880/µL, platelets 150,000/µL, serum urea 223 mg/dL, sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L; liver and thyroid function tests were normal. Ultrasound abdomen demonstrated hepatosplenomegaly and irregular, shrunken kidneys without hydronephrosis. Contrast‑enhanced CT of the chest and abdomen confirmed splenomegaly and retroperitoneal and axillary lymphadenopathy, with no mediastinal nodes, pulmonary consolidation, collapse, or cavitation. Fine‑needle aspiration of the axillary node was inconclusive, and endoscopic ultrasound‑guided aspiration of retroperitoneal nodes showed reactive lymphoid cells with few histiocytes. QuantiFERON‑TB Gold test was positive.

1. Malaria considered due to prolonged fever but excluded by negative serology. | "Serological tests for malaria... were negative"
2. Dengue considered as a febrile illness but excluded by negative serology. | "Serological tests for ... dengue... were negative"

Tuberculosis considered due to persistent fever, hepatosplenomegaly, axillary and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, and a positive QuantiFERON‑TB Gold test; supported as the most plausible cause. | "In view of persistent fever, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly and positive quantiferon gold test"

Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished tuberculosis from pyogenic abscesses and other infectious etiologies by (a) lack of response to broad‑spectrum antibiotics, (b) negative bacterial cultures and Gram stain, (c) positive tuberculin skin test, (d) exclusion of other endemic infections via serology, and (e) definitive detection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis DNA by PCR on aspirated pus despite negative AFB staining.
case_prompt:
A 22‑year‑old nonsmoker, nonalcoholic male from a middle‑class family in the midwestern part of Nepal was referred to our tertiary center with intermittent fever, pain in the left lower chest, occasional nausea and vomiting, anorexia, and weight loss of three‑week duration. Symptoms did not improve with two weeks of broad‑spectrum oral and then parenteral antibiotics at a local hospital. Fever was associated with chills and rigors. Left lower chest pain was continuous with radiation to the left shoulder. There was no associated cough, shortness of breath, altered bowel or bladder habits, jaundice, headache, vomiting, joint pain, or any skin nodules. There was no history of drug abuse or sexual promiscuity. There was no history of diabetes mellitus and no past or family history of TB.  

On examination, the patient's body temperature was 102 °F, pulse 100 beats per minute, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, regular. Chest examination showed tenderness in the left infra‑axillary region and normal bilateral vesicular breath sounds without any additional sounds. Cardiovascular examination revealed normal heart sounds without murmur. Abdominal examination showed a soft, tender left upper quadrant with Traube's space dullness; the spleen and liver were not palpable.  

Laboratory studies: complete blood count, liver and renal function tests, posteroanterior chest X‑ray, and echocardiography were normal. ESR was elevated at 58 mm/h. Purified protein derivative (PPD) was 12 mm. Three consecutive sputum samples were negative for acid‑fast bacilli (AFB). Spot serologic tests for HIV, hepatitis B, and hepatitis C were non‑reactive. Three consecutive bacterial blood cultures and a urine culture showed no growth. Serologic tests for malaria, leptospirosis, brucellosis, and leishmaniasis were negative.  

Imaging: abdominal ultrasound revealed a 5.3 × 4.0 × 3.5 cm hypoechoic lesion at the lower pole of the spleen communicating with a ~40 ml perisplenic collection, and a 3.9 × 3.0 × 2.8 cm collection at the superior pole also communicating with perisplenic fluid. Contrast‑enhanced CT of the abdomen showed two perisplenic hypodense collections (6.9 × 5.1 × 3.2 cm inferiorly and 5.2 × 4.0 × 3.0 cm superiorly) connected with splenic parenchymal collections, suggestive of multiple splenic abscesses with perisplenic extensions.  

The patient did not improve with three weeks of empiric parenteral broad‑spectrum antibiotics. Diagnostic and therapeutic ultrasound‑guided aspiration removed approximately 30 ml of pus, which was sent for microbiological and molecular examination for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Primary splenic tuberculosis considered because of prolonged fever, weight loss, positive tuberculin skin test, splenic abscesses in an endemic region, and lack of response to broad‑spectrum antibiotics. | "PPD was 12 mm." … "PCR for MTB was positive."
2. Pyogenic bacterial splenic abscess considered due to imaging of abscesses, but ruled out by negative blood, urine, and sputum cultures, negative Gram stain, and failure to respond to antibiotics. | "Three consecutive bacterial blood cultures and a urine culture showed no growth." … "The patient did not improve with three weeks of empiric parenteral broad‑spectrum antibiotics."
3. Brucellosis considered given systemic symptoms, but excluded by negative serology. | "Serologic tests for ... brucellosis ... were negative."
4. Leishmaniasis considered and excluded by negative serology. | "Serologic tests for ... leishmaniasis ... were negative."
5. Malaria and leptospirosis considered because of fever and were excluded by negative serology. | "Serologic tests for malaria, leptospirosis ... were negative."
6. HIV infection considered as a predisposing factor for atypical infections, but excluded by non‑reactive serology. | "Spot serological tests for human immunodeficiency virus ... were nonreactive."
7. Tuberculosis confirmed by molecular detection of MTB DNA in aspirated pus despite negative AFB staining, supporting a diagnosis of primary splenic TB. | "The pus was negative for AFB staining; however, PCR for MTB was positive."

case_prompt: A 47‑year‑old male surgeon presented on February 12, 2016, with fever. He was vaccinated against yellow fever. A thick blood smear was positive for malaria, and he was started on artemether‑lumefantrine. After six days there was no clinical improvement; his high‑grade fever and generalized weakness persisted, leading to hospitalization in a private room with dedicated nursing care. On day 6 after consultation he reported fever, chills, malaise, headaches, pharyngitis, hypoacusis, and diffuse abdominal pain. Laboratory studies revealed leukopenia (1,100 cells/mm³) and thrombocytopenia (65,000 /mm³). His epigastric pain worsened, and, based on a syndrome of abdominal pain with febrile illness, an exploratory laparotomy was performed, after which the operative wound began bleeding. He was air‑lifted to Cologne, Germany, on day 13; prior to evacuation he received two units of packed red blood cells because his hemoglobin had fallen to 6.8 g/dL with evidence of hemolysis. Despite intensive care in Germany, his condition deteriorated rapidly on the second day of admission, and he died on day 14.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Persistent fever despite appropriate antimalarial therapy raises suspicion for an alternative etiology beyond malaria. | "The thick smear performed was positive for malaria and received artemether/lumefantrine without any favorable clinical course after six days."
2. Development of leukopenia and thrombocytopenia is atypical for uncomplicated malaria and suggests a systemic process such as viral hemorrhagic fever or severe sepsis. | "Laboratory tests showed leukopenia (1,100 cells/mm³) and thrombocytopenia (65,000/mm³)."
3. Hemorrhagic manifestations—including operative wound bleeding, rapid drop in hemoglobin, and signs of hemolysis—point toward a hemorrhagic viral infection rather than uncomplicated malaria or uncomplicated postoperative infection. | "He was thus air‑lifted... his hemoglobin dropped to 6.8 g/dL with evidence of hemolysis symptoms."
4. The initial positive malaria smear could represent a coinfection or incidental finding, but the lack of response to therapy and the severe hematologic abnormalities make malaria an unlikely sole cause. | "without any favorable clinical course after six days."
5. Post‑operative bacterial infection was considered because of the laparotomy, but the rapid systemic deterioration and hemorrhagic picture are more consistent with a viral hemorrhagic fever. | "exploratory laparotomy was conducted, which was followed by a bleeding on the operative wound."

Imaging localized the process to bone marrow; histology demonstrated intracellular organisms, narrowing the differential to intracellular parasites. Definitive diagnosis was achieved by PCR confirmation of Leishmania DNA, distinguishing it from other intracellular pathogens or hematologic malignancies.
case_prompt:
In September 2016, a 60‑year‑old male Austrian patient presented with a three‑week history of fever of unknown origin, fatigue, and an unintentional weight loss of 6 kg. He had well‑controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus and hypothyroidism. Travel history included two‑week trips to southern Crete (September 2015) and southern Spain (May 2016).

Physical examination was unremarkable except for splenomegaly (7.2 × 16.4 cm) on abdominal sonography. Laboratory studies showed markedly elevated C‑reactive protein (94.2–188.9 mg/L), mild normocytic, hypochromic anemia (Hb 12.5 g/dL), mild thrombocytopenia (127 × 10³/µL), and a subtly elevated γ‑glutamyltransferase. The soluble interleukin‑2 receptor was increased (5156 pg/mL). Initial chest X‑ray, urine analysis, transthoracic and transesophageal echocardiography were normal.

Empiric antibiotics (initially ampicillin/sulbactam, later piperacillin/tazobactam plus vancomycin) yielded no clinical improvement. Over the next three weeks, bicytopenia progressed to severe pancytopenia requiring transfusions; lactate dehydrogenase rose to 1107 U/L, and liver enzymes (GGT, alkaline phosphatase, AST) increased. Fever persisted up to 40 °C.

Extensive infectious work‑up was negative: serial blood cultures, PCR for influenza, IgM serology for Puumala, Dobrava, and Hantaan viruses, PCR for cytomegalovirus and Epstein–Barr virus, leptospirosis antibody, malaria smear, interferon‑γ release assay for tuberculosis, and HIV antibody test. 

Positron emission tomography‑computed tomography demonstrated increased tracer uptake in both central and peripheral bone marrow. Bone‑marrow biopsy revealed numerous microorganisms within macrophages.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial sepsis considered but excluded because blood cultures remained negative and broad‑spectrum antibiotics failed to improve the patient | "Serial blood cultures were negative... Empiric antibiotic therapy... did not lead to improvement."
2. Tuberculosis evaluated due to fever and splenomegaly but ruled out by a negative interferon‑gamma release assay | "tuberculosis (negative interferon‑gamma release assay)."
3. HIV infection investigated as a cause of pancytopenia; testing was negative | "human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) (negative antibody)."
4. Viral etiologies (influenza, hantavirus, CMV, EBV) were excluded by negative PCR and IgM serologies | "tests for influenza (negative PCR), other viral infections (negative IgM antibody test for Puumala, Dobrava, and Hantaan virus, negative PCR for cytomegalovirus and Epstein‑Barr virus)."
5. Leptospirosis assessed due to travel history; serology was negative | "leptospirosis (negative antibody test)."
6. Malaria considered given febrile travel; peripheral smear was negative | "malaria (negative blood smear)."
7. Hematologic malignancy (e.g., lymphoma, leukemia) considered because of marrow PET uptake and pancytopenia; bone‑marrow biopsy showed only intracellular microorganisms without malignant cells | "Bone marrow biopsy revealed microorganisms within macrophages."
8. Visceral leishmaniasis confirmed after PCR detection of Leishmania DNA in peripheral blood and bone marrow, establishing the definitive diagnosis | "PCR from peripheral blood and bone marrow confirmed infection with Leishmania donovani."

case_prompt:
In February 2017, a Good Samaritan brought a 25‑year‑old waitress to the emergency department of Gulu Regional Referral and Teaching Hospital after she was found unconscious. On examination she was well hydrated, had full‑volume peripheral pulses, no conjunctival pallor or peripheral edema. Her Glasgow coma scale was 11/15 and Kernig’s sign was positive; pupils were equal, accommodative, and reactive. Vital signs: blood pressure 115/70 mmHg, pulse 100 bpm, respiratory rate 16/min, temperature 37.5 °C. Rapid malaria test was negative and random blood glucose was normal. After a few hours she regained consciousness and reported a progressive worsening headache without convulsions, fever, or visual changes; review of systems was otherwise non‑contributory.

Past medical history was notable for HIV infection diagnosed in November 2016, during which she was treated for cryptococcal meningitis (CM) after a CSF examination confirmed the diagnosis. She received fluconazole 1200 mg daily for two weeks, then 800 mg daily orally, and was started on tenofovir/lamivudine/efavirenz. She missed her follow‑up appointment, discontinued fluconazole and antiretroviral therapy.

Given the current presentation and history, a diagnostic lumbar puncture was performed to obtain cerebrospinal fluid for analysis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Prior cryptococcal meningitis and current subacute headache with meningeal irritation in an untreated HIV patient make recurrent CM the leading hypothesis | "From her presentation and PMH, a recurrence of CM was the most likely diagnosis."
2. Positive serum and CSF cryptococcal antigen assays together with numerous budding yeast cells on India‑ink stain confirm cryptococcal infection as the cause of meningitis | "Serum and CSF point‑of‑care lateral flow assays were both positive for cryptococcal antigen… Microscopic examination of an India ink preparation of the CSF demonstrated numerous budding yeast cells… consistent with morphologic identification of Cryptococcus species."

case_prompt:
A 20‑year‑old man with no past medical history presented to the emergency department with 7 days of fever, malaise, and arthralgia. On arrival he was febrile (39 °C); the remainder of the physical examination was normal. He reported ingesting unpasteurized camel’s milk, and serological testing for brucellosis was positive. Initial laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 145 g/L, white blood cells 7.6 × 10⁹/L (45.6 % lymphocytes, 49.2 % neutrophils), and platelets 4 × 10⁹/L. Chemistry revealed urea 3.6 mmol/L, creatinine 75.25 µmol/L, total bilirubin 16.1 µmol/L, ALT 48 IU/L, AST 52 IU/L. He denied using over‑the‑counter drugs, painkillers, or NSAIDs. He was advised to be admitted but left against medical advice after being prescribed doxycycline and rifampicin.

Two days later he returned with epistaxis, gingival bleeding, and hematuria. He was febrile (38.7 °C), blood pressure 110/75 mmHg, heart rate 72 beats/min. Examination revealed a non‑itchy flat purpuric rash on the lower extremities; cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, and neurologic exams were normal. Repeat CBC showed hemoglobin 128 g/L, white blood cells 4.9 × 10⁹/L (51.8 % lymphocytes, 41.1 % neutrophils), and platelets 2 × 10⁹/L. Peripheral smear demonstrated normal red and white cells, marked thrombocytopenia with occasional giant platelets and no platelet clumps. To exclude other causes of thrombocytopenia, malaria blood film, coagulation profile, fibrinogen level, antinuclear antibody, double‑stranded DNA antibody, and serologies for HBsAg, anti‑HCV, HIV, cytomegalovirus, and Epstein‑Barr virus were all unremarkable. Brucella agglutination test remained positive (titer 1 : 1280).
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Brucellosis as the underlying infection – exposure to unpasteurized camel milk and a positive serologic test support this diagnosis. | "A history of ingesting unpasteurized camel's milk was reported, and a serological test for brucellosis was positive."
2. Immune thrombocytopenic purpura secondary to infection – severe isolated thrombocytopenia with bleeding manifestations fits ITP, and the temporal relationship to brucellosis suggests a secondary cause. | "There was severe isolated thrombocytopenia (4000), but no evidence of skin or mucous membranes bleeding."
3. Malaria excluded – malaria can cause thrombocytopenia, but the malaria blood film was negative. | "malaria blood film ... were unremarkable."
4. Autoimmune etiologies (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus) excluded – negative ANA and anti‑dsDNA make these unlikely. | "antinuclerar antibody (ANA), double‑stranded DNA antibody (anti‑ds DNA) ... were unremarkable."
5. Viral infections (HIV, CMV, EBV, hepatitis B/C) excluded – serologies were negative. | "serological tests for HbsAg, anti‑HCV, HIV, cytomegalovirus, and Ebstein‑Barr virus all were unremarkable."
6. Drug‑induced thrombocytopenia excluded – patient denied use of over‑the‑counter drugs, painkillers, or NSAIDs. | "He denied use of any over‑the‑counter drugs, painkillers, or NSAIDs."
7. Bone‑marrow or malignant processes unlikely – peripheral smear showed normal red and white cell morphology, arguing against marrow infiltration. | "peripheral blood smear examination showed normal RBCs, WBCs morphology, and marked thrombocytopenia with occasional giant platelets and no platelet clumps."

case_prompt:
A 32‑year‑old HIV‑infected man presented with a 2‑week history of headache and fever and a 1‑day history of confusion. He had been receiving antiretroviral therapy (zidovudine, lamivudine, efavirenz) and co‑trimoxazole prophylaxis for five years, but admitted poor adherence to both ART and anti‑tuberculous medications. case_prompt:
A 65‑year‑old woman with a body mass index of 35.5 presented with an 8‑month history of progressive, mechanical left‑hip pain that was initially relieved by analgesics but had become disabling despite worsening walking distance. Physical examination revealed markedly diminished lateral rotation and abduction of the left hip; all other findings were normal. Anteroposterior and lateral pelvis radiographs demonstrated features of hip osteoarthritis, and total hip arthroplasty (THA) via a posterolateral approach was planned.

During the operation, after skin incision and subcutaneous hemostasis, a well‑circumscribed, 2.5‑cm‑diameter shell was discovered within the adipose tissue, approximately 5 cm thick. Incising the shell released a whitish, thick, oily‑appearing material that resembled pus. The lesion was isolated, the surrounding tissues appeared healthy, and the shell was resected for pathology. Specimens were sent for bacteriological analysis.

Cytobacteriological examination described a greasy appearance with epithelial and lymphocytic cells but no visible germs. Histology showed a fibrous wall with chronic inflammatory remodeling composed of lymphocytes and plasma cells, without necrotic centers.

Given these findings, the team interviewed the patient, who disclosed having received an intramuscular injection of an artemisinin‑derived compound on the right buttock for malaria two months earlier; a thick‑drop test had been positive before the injection, and oral treatment had followed. The surgical specimen was forwarded to a laboratory for confirmation of artemether by thin‑layer chromatography.

1. Septic or purulent collection considered because the intra‑operative material was white, thick, and oily, resembling pus; however, cultures showed no organisms and histology lacked necrosis, arguing against acute infection. | "Cytobacteriological examination ... there were no visible germs." 
2. Prosthetic joint infection considered given the planned THA, but the lesion was localized to gluteal fat, not joint tissue, and microbiology was negative. | "All the neighborhood tissues were healthy (very localized lesion)." 
3. Osteomyelitis or deep tissue malignancy considered due to chronic inflammation, but lack of necrotic centers and absence of atypical cells on histology made these unlikely. | "Histological examination ... fibrous wall with chronic inflammatory remodeling ... no necrosis centers." 
4. Foreign‑body reaction to a drug depot considered after patient recalled recent intramuscular artemisinin injection; the temporal relation and localized adipose deposit supported this hypothesis. | "The patient reported a notion of malaria ... treated with an intramuscular injection on the right buttock of the compounds derived from artemisinin." 
5. Confirmation of drug deposition pursued with thin‑layer chromatography; detection of artemether would substantiate the foreign‑body hypothesis. (Result not yet disclosed at the breakpoint.) | "The plate then shows an orange spot ... indicating that there was artemether in this human fat sample."

A 32‑year‑old man with no prior medical conditions presented to the emergency department in southwestern Nigeria with an acute onset of high‑grade intermittent fever with chills and rigors, headache, myalgia, abdominal pain, and vomiting. He had taken oral antimalarials, ciprofloxacin, and antipyretics without improvement. He worked outdoors as an agricultural research fellow.  

On examination he was febrile (38.9 °C), blood pressure 120/70 mmHg, pulse 92 bpm, respiratory rate 24/min; the remainder of the physical exam was normal. Initial labs showed leukocytes 7,090/µL (84.7% neutrophils), hemoglobin 14.5 g/dL, platelets 89,000/µL, prolonged APTT (15.2 s) and PT (5.3 s), INR 1.35, markedly elevated D‑dimer 224.6 µg/mL, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL, AST 223 IU/L, ALT 70 IU/L, and microscopic hematuria. Intravenous ciprofloxacin, metronidazole, and parenteral artesunate were started.  

The next day his temperature rose to 39.2 °C, pulse 102 bpm, and he developed right iliac fossa and suprapubic tenderness. Ciprofloxacin was switched to ceftriaxone and metoclopramide added for persistent vomiting.  

On hospital day 4 he reported rhinorrhea; exam now showed mildly inflamed pharynx, no significant lymphadenopathy, pulse 82 bpm, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 32/min, and reduced breath sounds in the middle and lower lung zones. Chest X‑ray revealed perihilar patchy opacities worse on the right, with additional patchy opacities in the right upper and lower zones. Azithromycin was added for presumed atypical community‑acquired pneumonia.  

The following day his temperature spiked to 40.5 °C despite antibiotics; pulse 100 bpm, blood pressure 130‑170/60‑100 mmHg, respiratory rate 62/min, SpO₂ 79‑81 % on room air. Percussion was dull over the right lower zone; auscultation revealed coarse crackles and rhonchi. Labs now showed worsening thrombocytopenia, increasing leukocytosis (11,720/µL), and persistent microscopic hematuria. Malaria blood smears were repeatedly negative. He received supplemental oxygen, loratadine, amlodipine, and was transferred to the ICU for respiratory support.  

In the ICU his dyspnea improved with oxygen by face mask (SpO₂ 93‑97 %). He remained febrile, tachypneic, and developed diarrhea with dark‑colored stools over the next three days.

Dengue infection considered because of high‑grade fever, thrombocytopenia, markedly elevated D‑dimer, transaminase rise, hemorrhagic diarrhea, and eventual positive RT‑PCR for dengue virus. | "On the 10th day of admission, a positive result for viral hemorrhagic fever screening using real-time RNA polymerase chain reaction panel detecting the dengue virus was obtained."

He self‑medicated with artemether‑lumefantrine for three days without improvement. Two weeks after symptom onset, he developed anuria and presented to the emergency unit on April 2. Sixteen days earlier he had contact with a confirmed COVID‑19 case. Laboratory studies revealed severe kidney dysfunction (urea 222 mg/dL, creatinine 15.9 mg/dL). Kidney ultrasound showed enlarged, echogenic kidneys with increased resistive index; no obstruction was seen. He was started on chloroquine, azithromycin, and vitamin C per national protocol. After five dialysis sessions, diuresis increased to 4 L/day and creatinine fell to 2 mg/dL; the clinical diagnosis was acute tubular necrosis. case_prompt:
A 38‑year‑old man, forest guard from a hilly Himalayan station, with a 15‑year history of schizophrenia treated with aripiprazole and trihexyphenidyl, presented to the emergency department after 7 days of high‑grade, intermittent fever accompanied by myalgia and headache. Four days into the fever he noted multiple painless rashes on the soles of both feet and ankles; the lesions were initially reddish and later darkened without gangrene formation or bleeding. He subsequently developed exertional dyspnea that progressed to dyspnea in the supine position, bilateral leg edema, generalized weakness, and oliguria for one day. There was no history of substance use, alcohol, smoking, or other comorbidities.

In an outside hospital, dengue NS1 antigen testing on day 3 of illness was positive, and the platelet count was 40 000/mm³. On arrival he was thin, pale, edematous, afebrile, mildly drowsy, and disoriented. Vital signs: HR 128 bpm (regular), BP 98/60 mm Hg, RR 30/min, SpO₂ 86 % on room air (improved to 92‑95 % with 4 L O₂). Physical examination revealed bilateral pitting pedal edema and multiple palpable, non‑tender purpuric macules (2‑8 mm) on both feet with fine scaling and post‑inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Peripheral pulses were palpable; JVP was not elevated. Chest auscultation showed bilateral basal fine crackles and occasional wheezes; heart sounds were normal with a regular rhythm. Abdominal exam disclosed mild tenderness in the right hypochondrium and epigastrium; liver and spleen were not enlarged.

Laboratory studies on day 8 of illness showed hemoglobin 9.4 g/dL (normocytic), leukocytes 7 900/mm³, platelet count 30 000/mm³, LDH 457 U/L (normal < 248), ESR 44 mm/h, CRP 14.2 mg/L, fibrin degradation products 12 mg/L, D‑dimer < 0.5 µg/mL. Renal function indicated acute kidney injury; liver tests revealed conjugated hyperbilirubinemia (total 2.83 mg/dL, direct 1.33 mg/dL), mild transaminitis, and hypoalbuminemia. NT‑pro‑BNP was markedly elevated (3114.7 pg/mL). Electrocardiogram showed sinus tachycardia; chest X‑ray suggested early pulmonary edema. Blood cultures were sterile. Serologies for malaria, scrub typhus, chikungunya, hepatitis B, hepatitis C, and HIV were negative; dengue IgM ELISA was positive. ADAMTS13 activity and complement levels could not be measured.

2. Malaria was excluded because specific testing was negative. | "Other infectious markers (malaria, scrub typhus, and chikungunya) were negative..."
3. Scrub typhus was excluded by negative serology. | "Other infectious markers (malaria, scrub typhus, and chikungunya) were negative..."
4. Chikungunya was excluded by negative serology. | "Other infectious markers (malaria, scrub typhus, and chikungunya) were negative..."
5. Bacterial sepsis was unlikely given sterile blood cultures. | "Blood cultures turned out to be sterile..."
6. Thrombotic microangiopathy (e.g., TTP/HUS) was considered because of thrombocytopenia, AKI, and elevated LDH, but ADAMTS13 testing was unavailable and D‑dimer was low, making overt TTP less likely. | "ADAMTS13 levels... could not be tested due to technical constraints." … "D‑dimer was <0.5."
7. Leukocytoclastic (cutaneous small‑vessel) vasculitis was identified on skin biopsy as the cause of the purpuric lesions, but the underlying trigger was sought; dengue was the only identified infectious trigger. | "skin biopsy … revealed … suggestive of leukocytoclastic vasculitis or CSVV."

case_prompt:
A 2‑month‑old infant was admitted in May 2018 to the children’s emergency department with a one‑month history of distressing, nocturnal cough and a three‑week history of high‑grade intermittent fever partially relieved by paracetamol. She was born at 28 weeks gestation by emergency lower‑segment Caesarean section after ante‑partum haemorrhage, weighing 1.65 kg, and had been managed in a special‑care baby unit for prematurity, neonatal sepsis, and jaundice before discharge at 1.8 kg. On presentation she appeared acutely ill, febrile (38.6 °C), mildly pale, dyspnoeic and tachypnoeic (RR 66/min) with SpO₂ 80 % on room air, heart rate 186 bpm. Weight was 3.7 kg (3rd percentile); length 50 cm and head circumference 38 cm (both <3rd percentile). Examination revealed tender hepatomegaly (6 cm) and splenomegaly (6 cm). Laboratory studies showed PCV 21 %, random glucose 4.7 mmol/L, HIV screen negative, total WBC 12.6 × 10⁹/L (neutrophils 65 %, lymphocytes 33 %), platelets 179 × 10⁹/L, malaria parasite test positive, Gene Xpert negative, Mantoux 0 mm. Chest X‑ray demonstrated hazy opacities in the right upper and middle lobes, left upper lobe opacities, and pneumatoceles. She received oxygen at 2 L/min and a transfusion of 60 mL settled cells (post‑transfusion PCV 25 %). Initial treatment included IV ceftriaxone and gentamicin; fever subsided and respiratory rate improved, and she was discharged after five days.

One week later she returned with worsening cough, fever, and respiratory distress. A provisional diagnosis of septicaemia with heart failure was made, with differential considerations of bronchopulmonary dysplasia and pulmonary tuberculosis. Empiric therapy was started with IV ceftriaxone, IV gentamicin, and oral azithromycin; furosemide and digoxin were added. On day 2, IV cloxacillin replaced gentamicin; on day 3 the child developed two generalized tonic‑clonic seizures lasting 1–2 min each, the second aborted with IV diazepam. Random glucose at the time was 2.9 mmol/L and SpO₂ fell to 67 %. Phenobarbitone and cautious IV fluids were commenced; supportive measures included repeat blood transfusion, nil per oral, oxygen, continued diuretics and digoxin. CSF analysis was not consistent with meningitis. Despite maximal therapy the infant remained in severe respiratory distress with intermittent hypothermia and died five days after readmission. Blood cultures were obtained on admission and on day 3 of the second stay (results were pending at the time of death).
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Malaria infection considered because “Malaria parasite test: positive,” yet fever and respiratory failure persisted despite antimalarial treatment, making malaria an unlikely sole cause. | "Malaria parasite test: positive"
2. Pulmonary tuberculosis evaluated due to chronic cough and radiographic infiltrates, but ruled out by “Gene Xpert: negative” and “Mantoux test: 0 mm,” and lack of typical cavitary lesions. | "Gene Xpert: negative, Mantoux test: 0 mm"
3. Bronchopulmonary dysplasia entertained given prematurity and chronic respiratory symptoms; however, the acute worsening, severe hypoxaemia, and systemic signs of sepsis were atypical for isolated BPD. | "to rule out bronchopulmonary dysplasia"
4. Bacterial sepsis from common pathogens (e.g., Gram‑negative rods) presumed, leading to empiric ceftriaxone, gentamicin, cloxacillin, but the lack of clinical improvement suggested an atypical or resistant organism. | "Empirical antibiotic (IV Ceftriaxone, IV Gentamicin, Suspension Azithromax) therapy were commenced."
5. Meningitis considered after seizures; CSF was “not in keeping with meningitis,” reducing its likelihood. | "CSF analysis was not in keeping with meningitis."
6. HIV infection excluded by “HIV screening was negative,” removing opportunistic infections from differential. | "HIV screening was negative"
7. The eventual identification of *T. ptyseos* from blood cultures (reported after death) provided the definitive etiologic agent, explaining persistent sepsis despite broad‑spectrum antibiotics. | "Blood culture yielded T. ptyseos."

case_prompt:
A 12‑year‑old girl presented with a one‑month history of sudden‑onset, progressively worsening headache associated with multiple episodes of vomiting and intermittent fever. There was no rash, seizure, loss of consciousness, or known contact with tuberculosis patients. Past medical history was unremarkable.

On examination she appeared ill. Vital signs: HR 64/min, RR 30/min, Temp 37.1 °C, BP 90/60 mm Hg. Chest exam revealed bilateral vesicular breath sounds without added sounds. Cardiovascular exam noted a pansystolic murmur. Abdomen was soft with mild hepatomegaly (2 cm). Neurologic assessment: GCS 14/15, pupils reactive 4 mm, early papilledema on funduscopy, flaccid tone, 4/5 strength in all limbs, intact sensation, grade II reflexes, downgoing plantar responses, and positive Kernig and Brudzinski signs. Working diagnosis was meningitis.

Laboratory studies: Hb 13.2 g/dL, WBC 13 000/mm³ (neutrophils 85 %, lymphocytes 10 %), platelets 211 000/mm³, ESR 31 mm/hr. Renal panel showed BUN 30 mg/dL, creatinine 0.46 mg/dL. HIV, HBsAg, and HCV serologies were negative. Chest x‑ray demonstrated bilateral consolidation; abdominal ultrasound confirmed mild hepatomegaly. MRI brain showed leptomeningeal enhancement and mild thickening without basal exudates or hydrocephalus, suggestive of meningoencephalitis. Echocardiogram identified a perimembranous ventricular septal defect (12 mm) partially closed by the tricuspid valve with mild tricuspid regurgitation.

Lumbar puncture: opening pressure 27 cm H₂O. CSF analysis – RBC 3 (0), WBC 204 (neutrophils 5 %, lymphocytes 95 %), glucose 46 mg/dL, protein 24 mg/dL, ADA 2.1 U/L. Gram stain, AFB stain, India‑ink preparation, and cultures were negative; cryptococcal antigen testing was unavailable. Blood and urine cultures were negative.

Empiric therapy with ceftriaxone 1.5 g IV q12h and vancomycin 100 mg IV q6h was started for 7 days. During this period she had a single seizure treated with antiepileptics and required supplemental oxygen. No clinical improvement occurred, and she was transferred to a second hospital.

On admission to the second facility she was semiconscious and admitted to the pediatric ICU. Additional investigations performed included leptospira IgM, brucella IgM, malaria antigen, and Mantoux tuberculin skin test, all of which were negative. Blood and urine cultures remained sterile, and sputum AFB smear and culture were negative. GeneXpert testing for Mycobacterium tuberculosis was not available.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Bacterial (pyogenic) meningitis considered initially due to acute headache and fever but deemed unlikely because CSF showed a lymphocyte‑predominant pleocytosis, normal protein, low opening pressure, and all cultures were negative. | "CSF ... WBC 204 cells ... lymphocyte 95% ... Gram stain, ... culture were negative."
2. Tuberculous meningitis entertained given chronic headache, but excluded based on lack of exposure, clear CSF, negative AFB stain, normal CSF ADA, and negative Mantoux test. | "There was no history of contact with active tubercular patients, CSF color was clear, CSF AFB staining was negative, and CSF ADA was not raised."
3. Viral meningitis considered but not supported by the presence of marked leptomeningeal enhancement on MRI and lack of a self‑limited clinical course; no viral PCR testing was performed. | "MRI brain showed enhancement and mild thickening of leptomeninges... features suggestive of meningoencephalitis."
4. Leptospirosis, brucellosis, and malaria were investigated due to the endemic setting but ruled out by negative serologies (leptospira IgM, brucella IgM, malaria antigens). | "Leptospira immunoglobulin M, brucella immunoglobulin M, malaria antigens ... all came out negative."
5. Other fungal infections were considered; initial India‑ink preparation at the first hospital was negative, but later microscopy revealed encapsulated yeast consistent with Cryptococcus spp. | "CSF India ink preparation showed Cryptococcus spp. (5 to 10 µm in size) with surrounding with a capsule."
6. Cryptococcal meningitis confirmed by positive cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) test on CSF, establishing the final diagnosis. | "CrAg test in CSF by enzyme immunoassay was positive."

case_prompt:
A 37‑year‑old nulliparous woman with a recent diagnosis of HIV infection (not on antiretroviral therapy) was admitted to the Mulago National Referral Hospital COVID‑19 Treatment Unit with a 3‑day history of worsening cough and dyspnea. She had a 2‑month history of productive mucoid cough, evening fevers, and weight loss, and a 5‑day history of anosmia, high‑grade intermittent fevers, headaches, altered mentation, an episode of loss of consciousness, and myalgias. Four days prior, a nasopharyngeal swab was positive for SARS‑CoV‑2 by RT‑PCR and rapid antigen test. She had tested HIV‑positive 8 days earlier and was not receiving antiretroviral therapy or cotrimoxazole prophylaxis.  

On presentation (day 0) she was critically ill: axillary temperature 38.5 °C, heart rate 168 bpm, respiratory rate 32 /min, blood pressure 132/76 mmHg, random blood glucose 8.7 mmol/L, and oxygen saturation 85–90 % on 5 L/min nasal prongs. Physical exam showed nasal flaring, intercostal recessions, and widespread bilateral coarse crepitations. She was restless with a Glasgow Coma Scale of 8/15 (E3 V2 M3). Neck rigidity with a positive Kernig’s sign was present. Other systems were unremarkable.  

Laboratory studies revealed a white‑blood‑cell count of 11.8 × 10³/µL (neutrophils 91.6 %, lymphocytes 4.5 %), hemoglobin 8.5 g/dL with MCV 67 fL, platelet count 300 × 10³/µL, and normal renal and liver biochemistry. Blood smear was negative for Plasmodium spp. and other haemoparasites. Blood group was B Rh D positive.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Advanced HIV infection predisposes to opportunistic CNS infections such as cryptococcal and tuberculous meningitis. | "A recent diagnosis of HIV infection not on anti‑retroviral therapy…"
2. Meningeal irritation (neck stiffness, positive Kernig’s sign) and altered mental status indicate meningitis. | "Her neck was stiff, with a positive Kernig's sign."
3. Absence of peripheral parasitemia makes malaria unlikely as a cause of fever and anemia. | "A blood smear was negative for Plasmodium and other haemoparasites."
4. Positive SARS‑CoV‑2 PCR/antigen test supports concurrent severe COVID‑19, which can cause respiratory failure but does not explain meningeal signs. | "Her nasopharyngeal swab for SARS‑CoV‑2 was positive on both reverse transcriptase‑polymerase chain reaction (RT‑PCR) and rapid antigen tests."
5. Bacterial meningitis is considered, but the patient’s profound lymphopenia (0.53 × 10³/µL) and chronic HIV infection make opportunistic fungal causes more likely. | "White blood cell count… with a lymphopenia of 0.53 (4.5 %)."
6. Tuberculous meningitis is a differential; however, definitive TB diagnostics (urine LAM, GeneXpert) were not yet available at this point. | *No quote available before breakpoint; authors later used urine LAM and GeneXpert to confirm TB.*
7. Cryptococcal meningitis is strongly suspected in HIV patients with CD4 < 50 cells/µL presenting with meningismus. | *Later confirmed:* "Her serum and cerebrospinal fluid cryptococcal antigen (CrAg) tests were positive."

case_prompt: A 41-year-old Sudanese woman presented to the emergency department with a 2‑day history of high‑grade fever (39.5 °C) accompanied by fatigue, nausea, and vomiting. Clinical evaluation and a blood test revealed a diagnosis of malaria, for which treatment was administered. In the following days her symptoms worsened, and she developed yellow sclera with laboratory findings of hemoglobin 5.5 g/dL and platelets 43 ×10³/µL. She was transferred to the rheumatology department at Omdurman Military Hospital for further evaluation. Apart from jaundice (bilirubin 3.2 mg/dL) physical examination was otherwise normal, although she noted a family history of Behçet’s disease in her sister. Shortly after admission she developed a severe headache, confusion, fever, an unrecordable blood pressure, and a Glasgow Coma Scale score of 9/15. The rapid‑response team was called and she was admitted to a high‑dependency unit, receiving six units of fresh frozen plasma and two units of red blood cells. After stabilization, additional laboratory investigations were ordered.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Persistent fever, jaundice, severe anemia and thrombocytopenia raised concern for an ongoing infectious or hematologic process beyond malaria. | "her symptoms worsened, in addition to yellow sclera and low hemoglobin (5.5 g/dL) and platelets (43 cells/mL)."
2. Neurologic deterioration (severe headache, confusion, GCS 9) with unrecordable blood pressure suggested possible central nervous system involvement, prompting consideration of severe infection, vasculitis, or thrombotic microangiopathy. | "she developed a severe headache associated with confusion and fever, her blood pressure was unrecordable, and her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 9/15."
3. Family history of Behçet’s disease led to initial consideration of Behçet’s‑related vasculitis, but lack of oral/genital ulcers and other classic signs made this less likely. | "She indicated that her sister had Behcet's disease."
4. Failure to improve with broad‑spectrum antibiotics (imipenem) and antiviral (acyclovir) implied that an infectious etiology was unlikely to be the sole cause. | "She was given imipenem 500 mg, acyclovir 75 mg..."
5. The combination of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (very low hemoglobin), severe thrombocytopenia, and neurologic impairment met criteria for thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, prompting plasmapheresis and immunosuppression. | "After her condition had stabilized, laboratory investigations were requested... A diagnosis of SLE and TTP was made."
6. Presence of auto‑immune features (e.g., positive serologies, though not detailed in the excerpt) supported systemic lupus erythematosus as the underlying trigger for TTP. | (implicit from the final diagnosis statement in the article).

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case centers on cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia (AIHA) following antimalarial therapy. AIHA is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases, while malaria (P. falciparum) appears only as a past infection without a current diagnostic work‑up. Therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.
2. Breakpoint: Include presentation up to the positive direct antiglobulin test (DAT) and the imaging showing splenomegaly with infarcts, but stop before the authors’ discussion of the presumed drug‑induced mechanism and treatment response. This provides sufficient clinical, laboratory, and imaging data for learners to infer AIHA without revealing the authors’ final interpretation.
3. Analytic Distinctions: The authors ruled out recurrent malaria (negative parasitemia), hereditary hemolytic disorders (normal G6PD, normal hemoglobin electrophoresis), infectious triggers (negative or non‑specific serologies for Mycoplasma, CMV, EBV, Parvovirus B19, hepatitis, HIV, Coxiella, etc.), and systemic autoimmunity (negative ANA/ENA/RF). The decisive finding was a positive DAT for C3d, supporting cold AIHA, and the lack of response to transfusion reinforced an immune‑mediated process.
case_prompt: On December 31, 2019, a 42‑year‑old Caucasian male presented to the emergency department of Nice University Hospital with left‑upper‑quadrant abdominal pain. His past medical history included colon cancer cured 10 years earlier and uncomplicated Plasmodium falciparum malaria diagnosed on December 13, 2019, after return from Togo; he had completed a 3‑day course of dihydroartemisinin/piperaquine 15 days prior to this visit. Initial laboratory testing showed macrocytic anemia with hemoglobin 5.4 g/dL, elevated bilirubin (45 µmol/L), undetectable haptoglobin (<0.1 g/L), LDH 2,835 U/L, and reticulocytes 297 g/L, suggesting hemolysis. Peripheral smear was not described. Malaria parasitemia was negative. Computed tomography demonstrated splenomegaly with several areas of splenic infarction. Physical examination revealed left hypochondrial tenderness and mucocutaneous pallor. Direct antiglobulin test (DAT) was positive for anti‑C3d. Autoimmune serologies (ANA, ENA, rheumatoid factor) were negative, as were serologic tests for EBV, hepatitis B, C, E, HIV, HTLV‑1, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Coxiella burnetii. Cytomegalovirus IgM and IgG were positive but PCR for viral DNA was negative. Mycoplasma pneumoniae IgM and IgG were positive without seroconversion, and Parvovirus B19 IgM/IgG were near the cutoff without compatible symptoms. Hemoglobin electrophoresis and G6PD activity were normal.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Recurrent malaria considered but excluded because “Parasitemia was negative” and prior parasitemia had cleared to <0.025 % by day 3 of treatment.  
2. Hereditary hemolytic disorders (e.g., sickle cell, G6PD deficiency) ruled out by “Hemoglobin electrophoresis analysis and G6PD testing were within the normal range.”  
3. Autoimmune systemic disease excluded as “Autoimmune assays (antinuclear antibodies, ANAs, extractable nuclear antigen, ENA, rheumatoid factor) were negative.”  
4. Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection deemed unlikely because “the serological monitoring did not show seroconversion and therefore did not support an acute infection.”  
5. Cytomegalovirus infection not active: “CMVIgM and IgG antibodies were both positive, but viral DNA detection in the blood by PCR was negative.”  
6. Parvovirus B19 infection not supported: “Parvovirus B19 IgM and IgG antibodies were close to the positive cutoff, but the patient did not have any consistent symptoms.”  
7. EBV, hepatitis B/C/E, HIV, HTLV‑1, Chlamydia pneumoniae, and Coxiella burnetii excluded by “serological tests were negative.”  
8. Lymphoproliferative or plasma‑cell disorder excluded by normal protein electrophoresis and immunofixation: “Blood protein electrophoresis and immunofixation were normal.”  
9. Drug‑induced immune hemolysis suggested by temporal relationship to antimalarial therapy and positive DAT: “DAT was positive for anti‑C3d, leading to the diagnosis of cold autoimmune hemolytic anemia.”

case_prompt:
A 47‑year‑old Asian Indian man with no significant past medical history presented to a Midwestern United States hospital four days after arriving from India with fever and diffuse body aches. He reported that his mother had recently been diagnosed with dengue in India. He mentioned that his home air‑conditioning unit, a known source of stagnant water for mosquitoes, had been turned off for the past two months. He denied petechiae, hematuria, hematemesis, or melena on admission.

Initial laboratory studies showed creatine kinase 999 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase 663 U/L, platelet count 41 K/µL, D‑dimer 2664 ng/mL, and AST 141 U/L. Peripheral smear was negative for malaria, and Lyme serology was negative.

On hospital day 2 the platelet count fell to 11 K/µL; he received one unit of platelets with a transient rise to 18 K/µL, then dropped again to 10 K/µL within six hours. Infectious disease and hematology‑oncology advised against further platelet transfusion unless counts fell below 10 K/µL.

On day 3 petechiae appeared on his lower extremities. Platelet counts continued to fluctuate between 11 K/µL and 18 K/µL over the next few days. From day 5 onward, platelet counts began to improve, creatine kinase normalized, and petechiae resolved by day 7. He was discharged on day 7 with a platelet count of 35 K/µL and no bleeding episodes.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Dengue infection considered likely given recent travel to an endemic area, a family member with confirmed dengue, severe thrombocytopenia, elevated liver enzymes, and CK elevation. | "Two weeks later, his dengue fever antibody IgG resulted positive with a titer of 7.07 ISR."
2. Malaria excluded because peripheral blood smear showed no parasites. | "Peripheral smear was negative for malaria."
3. Lyme disease excluded by negative serology. | "Lyme serology was negative."
4. Other causes of thrombocytopenia (e.g., immune thrombocytopenic purpura, drug‑induced) deemed less likely given the acute febrile illness, rapid platelet fluctuation, and spontaneous recovery without specific therapy. | "Platelet counts continued to fluctuate... continued improvement noted…"

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s definitive diagnosis is visceral leishmaniasis (kala-azar), which maps to **leishmaniasis** on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. No other SELECTED disease is the primary active problem.
2. Best breakpoint: Include all presenting information up to the point just before the metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS) result that explicitly identified Leishmania DNA. This provides the fever, diarrhea, prior travel, laboratory abnormalities, imaging findings, and the broad differential (sepsis, tumor, decompensated cirrhosis) without revealing the pathogen.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors first considered common infectious and non‑infectious causes (sepsis, tumor, cirrhosis) based on fever, cytopenias, and imaging; they ruled these out by lack of response to broad antibiotics, negative cultures for pathogenic organisms, and negative serologies. Definitive identification was achieved only after mNGS detected Leishmania spp., confirmed by rK39 serology, leading to the final diagnosis of kala‑azar.
case_prompt:
Patient 1: Male, 47 years old, technical staff. He presented on December 28, 2020 with “recurrent fever for 4 months with aggravation accompanied with diarrhea for 1 month.” Approximately 4 months earlier, he developed sudden fever up to 39.9 °C, usually in the afternoon, resolving after several hours, and was associated with headache, myalgia, and nausea. case_prompt:
A 38‑year‑old South African woman presented to a district hospital in Durban with progressive, painless bilateral visual loss beginning on 10 March 2020. She reported mild, intermittent headaches relieved by simple analgesia; systemic enquiry was otherwise non‑contributory. She was diagnosed with HIV in 2006, started ART in 2012, and was switched to second‑line ART in 2020 after virological failure. On initial ophthalmic assessment she had bilateral panuveitis with macular oedema and disc pallor with non‑perfused vessels; topical and sub‑Tenon’s steroids plus bilateral bevacizumab injections resolved the macular oedema. HIV viral load was 208 806 copies/mL (15 Jan 2020) rising to 237 000 copies/mL (15 Mar 2020); CD4 count was 39 cells/µL.

She was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) on the basis of typical chest radiographic changes and began anti‑TB therapy on 18 April 2020, after which her visual loss worsened. By 25 May 2020 she had no perception of light in either eye; fundus examination showed resolving macular oedema, disc pallor and extensive non‑perfused vessels.

She was admitted in February 2021; ART adherence was reported, HIV viral load was 136 copies/mL and CD4 count 132 cells/µL. No history of eye trauma, surgery, or family ocular disease was noted. She denied toxic exposures, swam in rivers, and previously worked as a domestic worker.

On examination she was obese; vital signs were normal. Visual acuity was 6/60 (right) and 1/60 (left) with no pinhole improvement. Anterior segment revealed bilateral pigmented keratic precipitates, anterior chamber cells, vitreous cells, and lenticular opacities. Fundus showed bilateral optic disc pallor, macular exudates, retinal vasculitis with extensive non‑perfused vessels. Chest radiograph was normal. Brain CT demonstrated a small focus of nodular irregular thickening adjacent to the right optic nerve insertion, suggestive of an inflammatory lesion, non‑benign lesion, haemorrhage, or artefact; no periventricular plaques, calcifications, infarcts, or pathological enhancement were seen.

Laboratory studies: white blood cell count 7.26 × 10⁹/L with eosinophils 5.70% (0.41 × 10⁹/L); CRP 47 mg/L, ESR 93 mm/hr; serum ACE 101 U/L (reference 8‑52), rheumatoid factor 13.0 IU/mL (negative ANA and ANF); hepatitis screen negative; vitamin B12 and folate normal. Syphilis serology negative (TPHA, FTA‑ABS). HSV IgM negative. CMV IgM negative. Toxoplasma gondii IgM ELISA negative. Anaerobic and aerobic blood cultures sterile. Lumbar puncture normal; liver ultrasound showed no cystic lesions.

1. Tuberculosis ocular involvement considered because of concurrent pulmonary TB but visual loss progressed after anti‑TB therapy and ocular findings (non‑perfused retinal vessels, disc pallor) were not typical for ocular TB; chest radiograph later normal. | "She was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis (PTB) ... after which she noticed worsening of the loss of vision in both eyes."

4. Syphilis was evaluated because it can cause uveitis; serology (TPHA, FTA‑ABS) was negative, ruling it out. | "Syphilis serology tests were negative (Treponema pallidum haemagglutinin assay, fluorescent treponemal antibody absorption test)."

7. Sarcoidosis considered because of elevated ACE; however ACE elevation was modest, ANA and RF were negative, and there were no systemic sarcoid manifestations, making it less likely. | "Serum Angiotensin Converting Enzyme (SACE) ... were weakly positive, at 101 U/L... Anti‑nuclear antibodies and anti‑nuclear factor were negative."

case_prompt:
A previously healthy 20‑year‑old woman presented after a generalized tonic‑clonic seizure that occurred during sleep deprivation. Neurologic examination and vital signs were normal. Laboratory studies were unremarkable except for an elevated C‑reactive protein of 45.8 mg/L (reference 0–6 mg/L). She denied fever, upper respiratory, urinary, or gastrointestinal symptoms but reported hip pain. Plain radiographs of the chest, hips, and lumbar spine were normal. EEG showed generalized epileptiform activity, and levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily was started. Brain MRI revealed multiple ring‑enhancing lesions. An infectious work‑up was initiated with albendazole for a presumed diagnosis of neurocysticercosis, although serologic testing was not performed because it was not readily available.

Four weeks into albendazole therapy, she developed new‑onset fever while continuing the antiparasitic regimen. She denied cough, anorexia, weight loss, or night sweats. Neurologic examination remained normal, without signs of raised intracranial pressure or meningitis, and seizures remained controlled on levetiracetam. A nasopharyngeal PCR test for coronavirus was negative, and thoracic imaging was unremarkable. Repeat brain MRI showed no change compared with the prior study.

Given concern for Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, a QuantiFERON‑TB Gold test was performed and was positive, indicating prior TB exposure. MRI of the right hip demonstrated active severe sacroiliitis. Physical examination identified a newly enlarged anterior cervical lymph node.

Neurocysticercosis considered because of multiple ring‑enhancing brain lesions on MRI, a typical imaging pattern for NCC; however, serologic confirmation was lacking and the lesions did not improve after four weeks of albendazole. | "Considering an infectious etiology, the patient was referred ... with a probable diagnosis of NCC... serological tests were not performed because they were not readily available."

Tuberculosis raised due to lack of radiologic resolution, positive interferon‑γ release assay, sacroiliitis, and cervical lymphadenopathy, all compatible with extrapulmonary TB. | "With a suspicion of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection, QuantiFERON‑TB Gold test was performed and resulted positive ... MRI of the hip revealed active severe sacroiliitis on the right side. An enlarged lymph node was newly detected in the anterior cervical region."
3. COVID‑19 infection excluded because nasopharyngeal PCR was negative and the patient had no respiratory symptoms. | "A polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test for coronavirus was negative."

Other bacterial or viral meningitis/encephalitis deemed unlikely because the patient had no fever at initial presentation, normal CSF studies were not reported, and repeat imaging showed no new meningeal enhancement. | "She denied having cough, loss of appetite, weight loss or night sweats. Her neurologic examination was normal without any sign of increased intracranial pressure or meningeal irritation."

case_prompt:
A 68‑year‑old man was admitted for a three‑month history of cough with white sputum, chest tightness, shortness of breath, and numbness of both lower limbs. He had a 50‑year smoking history (20 cigarettes/day) but quit five months earlier. Physical examination showed rough breath sounds without rhonchi or moist rales; no lymphadenopathy or cardiac/abdominal abnormalities.

Initial work‑up (March 2022) revealed a 12.6 × 7.6 cm mixed‑density mass in the left upper lobe with bronchial obstruction and multiple small patchy and nodular high‑density shadows in adjacent lung. Cranial MRI showed a presumed cavernous hemangioma. Tracheoscopy demonstrated a cauliflower‑like neoplasm blocking the left upper lobe bronchial orifice. Tumor markers were modestly elevated (CEA 6 mg/ml, CA125 88.18 U/ml, CYFRA 21‑1 12.91 ng/ml, NSE 33.72 ng/ml). Routine blood tests, bone scan, biochemistry, coagulation, echocardiogram, and ECG were unremarkable. Bronchoscopic biopsy confirmed moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma (CK5/6+, P40+, P63+, Ki‑67 50‑60%). Etiologic tests for bacteria, fungus, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Pneumocystis, Actinomyces, Nocardia, and cytomegalovirus were negative.

Because the tumor was unresectable, he received two cycles of docetaxel‑cisplatin chemotherapy (15 March and 5 April 2022). During the second cycle he developed severe gastrointestinal toxicity and bone‑marrow suppression (WBC 1.3 × 10⁹/L, neutrophils 0.23 × 10⁹/L). He then received a single dose of camrelizumab immunotherapy (25 April 2022). On 21 May 2022 he began coughing up ≈20 mL of blood‑streaked sputum. A chest CT on 22 May 2022 showed that the previously noted left‑upper‑lobe cancer had regressed, but multiple small nodules and patchy high‑density shadows in both lungs were more extensive than before, a pattern that could not exclude pneumonia or infection associated with immune checkpoint inhibition.

1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case centers on a chronic actinomycetoma initially presumed to be caused by Nocardia spp. Nocardia infection (nocardiosis) is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list.
