Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors first described clinical ulcerative lesions superimposed on psoriasis, performed repeated biopsies, used histology, clonality studies, immunofluorescence, and broad infectious serologies/PCR to exclude lymphoma, syphilis, HIV, borreliosis, TB, and autoimmune disease. Only after these were negative did they identify Leishmania amastigotes on multiple stains and confirm species by culture and PCR, establishing cutaneous leishmaniasis as the cause.
case_prompt:
A 42‑year‑old Italian man with a 20‑year history of plaque psoriasis and psoriatic arthritis presented with numerous ulcerations or nodules within his psoriatic lesions that had appeared 6 months earlier. He had been receiving subcutaneous methotrexate (25 mg weekly) for 9 years and adalimumab (40 mg every other week) for 7 years; topical therapy in the weeks before admission included halometasone 0.05 % plus triclosan 1 % cream and calcipotriol plus betamethasone dipropionate foam. He was obese (BMI 39 kg/m²). Examination showed extensive erythemato‑squamous psoriatic plaques (PASI 16.6) with erosive, partly ulcerating plaques and nodules, some covered by brown crusts, on the right forearm, right knee, left flank, and abdomen. No lymphadenopathy or other systemic findings were noted.

Initial histopathology from an external lesion biopsy reported dermal T‑cell infiltrates without evidence of malignancy. Two repeat biopsies from morphologically different lesions on the right forearm and right flank demonstrated interface dermatitis with pseudolymphomatous infiltrates, epidermal thickening, follicular hyperparakeratosis, and superficially accentuated perivascular and periadnexal lymphocytic infiltrates dominated by T cells. Tissue clonality analysis showed polyclonal IgH and TCR γ‑chain gene expression, excluding lymphoma. Direct immunofluorescence was negative for IgG, IgM, IgA, and C3 deposits. Syphilis serology, performed because of numerous plasma cells in the tissue, was negative. Serologic and PCR testing for HIV infection, borreliosis, and tuberculosis were also negative. Antibodies against extractable nuclear antigens were absent, and complement levels were within normal limits.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Cutaneous lymphoma considered due to pseudolymphomatous infiltrates; excluded by polyclonal IgH and TCR γ‑chain gene expression. | "Tissue clonality analyses demonstrated polyclonal IgH and TCR gamma chain gene expression, thus excluding lymphoma."
2. Secondary syphilis considered because plasma cells were present; excluded by negative serology. | "Syphilis serology, carried out due to numerous plasma cells in the tissue, yielded negative results."
3. HIV‑associated opportunistic skin disease considered; excluded by negative HIV antibody/PCR testing. | "Moreover, an HIV infection ... were ruled out by negative antibody or PCR tests."
4. Borreliosis (Lyme disease) considered as a possible cause of ulcerative lesions; excluded by negative testing. | "...borreliosis ... were ruled out by negative antibody or PCR tests."
5. Cutaneous tuberculosis considered; excluded by negative PCR/serology. | "...tuberculosis were ruled out by negative antibody or PCR tests."
6. Autoimmune connective‑tissue disease considered (e.g., lupus); excluded by negative ANA and normal complement. | "A serum sample was negative for antibodies against (extractable) nuclear antigens. Complement factors were within normal ranges."
7. Primary psoriatic ulceration or drug‑induced ulceration considered given long‑standing psoriasis and biologic therapy; deemed less likely after histology showed interface dermatitis with plasma cells and after infectious causes were systematically excluded, prompting further investigation. | No direct quote; inference from overall work‑up described above.
8. Cutaneous leishmaniasis ultimately identified by intracellular amastigotes on multiple stains, confirmed by culture and PCR, establishing the definitive diagnosis. | "In hematoxylin‑eosin (Figure 1C), Giemsa (Figure 1D) and Feulgen stains, intracellular Leishmania amastigotes with kinetoplasts were seen, which were identified by culture, miniexon PCR and restriction fragment length polymorphism‑analysis as L. infantum."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient’s presentation ultimately proved to be HIV infection (hiv_aids), which is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. The case report’s narrative confirms HIV as the primary diagnosis, with associated HIV‑associated vacuolar myelopathy and dementia.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Include all clinical data up to, but not including, the statement of a positive HIV test. This provides the progressive paraparesis, cognitive dysfunction, pancytopenia, CSF pleocytosis, MRI findings, and exclusion of other differentials, allowing learners to reason toward HIV infection before the result is disclosed.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors systematically ruled out compressive spinal/brain lesions (normal MRI), vitamin‑B12 deficiency (normal B12 level), systemic lupus erythematosus (clinical/lab exclusion), and other opportunistic infections (negative toxoplasma and syphilis serologies) before ordering HIV testing, thereby narrowing the differential to HIV‑associated disease.
case_prompt:
A 35‑year‑old woman presented with a 3‑month history of progressive weakness in both lower limbs, beginning in the right leg and later involving the left. The weakness was non‑fluctuating, culminating in a bedridden state. She also reported a painless oral ulcer of six‑month duration, hair loss, weight loss, and urinary and fecal incontinence for the past month, with recent cognitive decline (poor attention, disorientation, forgetfulness). No upper‑limb weakness, dysphagia, or dyspnea was noted. Past obstetric history included a cesarean section 12 years earlier; she had received three units of blood at that time. She denied fever, joint pain, sensory symptoms, photosensitivity, Raynaud’s phenomenon, chronic diarrhea, recent travel, or exposure to unpasteurized dairy. Menstruation had ceased for six months. She had no prior medical or surgical illnesses.

On examination she was cachectic, anemic, and showed glossitis with oral thrush and alopecia. Neurologically, lower‑limb tone was increased, muscle power 2/5 (MRC), with marked wasting, hyperreflexia, clonus, and bilateral extensor plantar responses. Upper limbs were normal; cranial nerves, cerebellar tests, and fundus examination were unremarkable. Cognitive testing using the International HIV Dementia Scale yielded a total score of 2, fulfilling criteria for HIV‑associated dementia.

Laboratory studies revealed pancytopenia with normocytic normochromic anemia, mildly elevated transaminases, normal thyroid function, normal vitamin B12 (669 pg/mL), and negative serologies for toxoplasmosis and syphilis. CSF analysis showed clear fluid with pleocytosis and elevated protein. Brain MRI demonstrated generalized, non‑age‑appropriate atrophy; spinal MRI showed no focal lesions or cord enhancement.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Compressive spinal or intracranial lesion – Imaging showed no focal compressive pathology; spinal MRI was normal and brain MRI revealed only diffuse atrophy. | "Spinal MRI ... revealed no significant lesion. No contrast enhancement was noted anywhere in the cord."
2. Vitamin B12 deficiency – Serum B12 level was within normal limits, ruling out B12‑related myelopathy. | "normal vitamin B12 level (669 pg/ml)."
3. Systemic lupus erythematosus – Clinical features and investigations did not support lupus; the authors explicitly excluded it. | "After any compressive lesion ... Vit‑B12 deficiency and lupus were excluded."
4. Toxoplasma infection – Serologic screening was negative, making cerebral toxoplasmosis unlikely. | "negative screens for toxoplasmosis and syphilis."
5. Syphilis – Serology negative, excluding neurosyphilis as a cause of neurologic decline. | "negative screens for toxoplasmosis and syphilis."
6. HIV infection – The constellation of progressive paraparesis, HAND‑compatible cognitive impairment, pancytopenia, CSF pleocytosis, and unexplained weight loss, together with exclusion of other differentials, pointed toward HIV as the unifying diagnosis. | "Then we sent for an HIV test, and it came as positive. Her absolute CD4 count was 54/microL."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient has confirmed HIV infection (stage II) with reactive anti‑HIV serology, which is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list (hiv_aids). Though the report also discusses secondary syphilis, ocular syphilis, hepatitis B, these are OUT_OF_SCOPE. Therefore the teaching focus will be on diagnosing HIV infection.
2. Breakpoint: Present the patient’s demographics, risk history, cutaneous and oral lesions, and the initial serologic work‑up (including anti‑HIV, HBsAg, TPHA, VDRL) up to—but stopping before—the authors’ statement that the oral lesions represent a “mucous patch” and before any treatment description. This provides enough data (reactive anti‑HIV test) to deduce HIV infection without revealing the syphilis diagnosis.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors identified HIV infection based on a documented reactive anti‑HIV immunoserology performed two weeks prior. They used serologic tests (TPHA, VDRL) and HBsAg to support concurrent infections (syphilis, hepatitis B) and distinguished the oral lesions as mucous patches of secondary syphilis, later responding to chlorhexidine mouthwash.
case_prompt: A 35‑year‑old man with a known diagnosis of HIV stage II was referred to the Oral Medicine Service for multiple skin and oral lesions. He reported a long‑standing history of alcohol use (age 15–29) and recent unprotected intercourse with both men and women over the past three years. Physical examination revealed numerous confluent, irregular, well‑defined papules and excoriated macules with hypopigmented areas on the chest, abdomen, back, and extremities. Intraorally, there were several irregular, painless ulcers on the palate with white margins and a yellow‑reddish base. Serologic testing performed two weeks earlier showed a reactive anti‑HIV assay, reactive hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg), a reactive Treponema pallidum hemagglutination assay (TPHA) with a titer of 1:10,240, and a reactive quantitative VDRL with a titer of 1:256.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. HIV infection confirmed by serology | "Immunoserological examination of anti‑HIV two weeks ago was reactive."
2. Secondary syphilis considered because of mucocutaneous lesions and high TPHA/VDRL titers | "TPHA titer was reactive with titer 1:10,240, and quantitative VDRL was reactive with titer 1:256."
3. Hepatitis B infection identified by surface antigen positivity | "Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) chromatography was reactive."
4. Neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis, and atypical optic neuritis raised due to neurologic/ocular involvement, but not substantiated by the data presented up to the breakpoint | "diagnosed with secondary syphilis, suspected neurosyphilis, ocular syphilis, and atypical optic neuritis."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case’s primary diagnostic focus is necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis (NUG), which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases. Although HIV infection (hiv_aids) is present, it is already established in the past‑medical history and not the lesion’s diagnostic work‑up. Therefore the target diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.  
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Include all presenting information up to the description of the oral findings and laboratory results, but stop before the authors state the definitive oral diagnoses (“The lesions on the gingiva were diagnosed with necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis…”). This provides sufficient signs and labs for the learner to infer the oral condition without revealing the label.  
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors differentiated NUG from other infectious or systemic causes by (a) the characteristic necrotic gray‑white plaque, bleeding, and pain in an immunocompromised host; (b) the presence of linear gingival erythema distinct from the necrotic area; and (c) exclusion of Mycobacterium tuberculosis by a negative assay, supporting an ulcerative gingival process rather than TB‑related oral disease.
case_prompt:
A 29‑year‑old man was referred by the Department of Internal Medicine regarding lesions in his oral cavity. He complained of pain in the lower anterior jaw gum and lower lip for one week and reported fever over the prior two weeks. He had been diagnosed by the internist with HIV stage IV with wasting syndrome, hypothyroidism, latent syphilis, chronic hepatitis B, moderate dehydration due to inadequate intake, stage 1 acute kidney injury, inflammatory anemia, and malnutrition.  

Extra‑oral examination showed exfoliative, pale‑appearing lips.  
Intra‑oral examination revealed multiple irregular painful erosions on the lower labial mucosa. The anterior mandibular gingiva was edematous, bled readily, and displayed an excruciating grayish‑white plaque in the region of teeth 33 to 43. On the upper anterior gingiva, reddish bands appeared on the attached gingiva of teeth 11 and 21.  

Laboratory testing demonstrated a reactive TPHA (titer 1:5120) and reactive VDRL (titer 1:64), reactive hepatitis B e antigen and HBsAg, non‑reactive anti‑HCV. Examination for Mycobacterium tuberculosis using the assay method did not detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacteria.  
The patient had been given azithromycin by internal medicine for a systemic infection and was instructed to irrigate with 1.5 % hydrogen peroxide, rinse with saline, and use 0.2 % chlorhexidine gluconate three times daily while maintaining oral hygiene.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. The necrotic, painful, gray‑white gingival plaque with bleeding is characteristic of necrotizing ulcerative gingivitis, especially in an immunocompromised host. | "excruciating grayish‑white plaque in the region of teeth 33 to 43"  
2. The linear reddish bands on the attached gingiva of the maxillary incisors are typical of linear gingival erythema, another HIV‑associated oral manifestation. | "reddish bands appeared on the attached gingiva of teeth 11 and 21"  
3. Tuberculosis was considered but excluded because microbiologic assay did not detect Mycobacterium tuberculosis. | "Examination of Mycobacterium tuberculosis using the Assay method did not find Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacteria"  
4. Syphilis serology was positive (reactive TPHA and VDRL), yet the oral lesions were not described as gummatous or typical of secondary syphilis, and the patient’s syphilis was classified as latent. | "reactive TPHA with titer 1:5120 and reactive VDRL with titer 1:64" (implying latent status)  
5. Hepatitis B infection was present, but hepatic disease does not produce the described necrotic gingival lesions, supporting an oral‑specific diagnosis. | "reactive hepatitis B e antigen (HBeAg), reactive HBsAg"

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case ultimately confirms pulmonary tuberculosis, which is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Therefore the target diagnosis is tuberculosis.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Include all clinical data up to the PET‑CT findings that demonstrated FDG‑avid hilar lymph nodes and left‑lung involvement, but stop before the bronchoscopy result that yielded Mycobacterium tuberculosis on smear and culture. This provides sufficient clues (neurologic syndrome, negative infectious/autoimmune work‑up, pulmonary FDG uptake) to allow the learner to arrive at tuberculosis without revealing the definitive microbiologic confirmation.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors systematically ruled out autoimmune encephalopathy (negative anti‑NAE), paraneoplastic syndromes (negative antibody panel and extensive cancer screening), viral encephalitis (negative PCR), and other bacterial/fungal infections (negative cultures and CSF studies). The persistent FDG‑avid pulmonary lesions on PET‑CT shifted suspicion toward an infectious etiology, prompting bronchoscopy that confirmed Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
case_prompt:
On admission the patient was alert and oriented (Glasgow Coma Scale E4V5M6). Vital signs were blood pressure 102/56 mmHg, heart rate 66 beats/min, peripheral oxygen saturation 98% on ambient air, respiratory rate 12 breaths/min, temperature 37.2 °C; body mass index 19.2 kg/m². Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable: lungs clear, normal heart sounds, no murmurs. Abdomen was soft without tenderness or organomegaly. Neurologic exam showed intact cranial nerves, normal motor strength, and preserved pinprick, temperature, proprioception, and vibration sensation. Reflexes were normal (Babinski negative, Romberg negative). Gait was wide‑based with tandem gait abnormality; finger‑nose‑finger testing revealed bilateral dysmetria, and diadochokinesis was slowed bilaterally.

Laboratory studies: white blood cell count 4,600/µL (neutrophils 2,760/µL), hemoglobin 12.6 g/dL, platelets 238,000/µL, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 6 mm/hr. Vitamin B1, B12, E, and folic acid levels were normal; syphilis serology was negative. Thyroid function tests were within normal limits, but anti‑thyroid peroxidase antibodies were elevated at 125 IU/mL. Serum anti‑N‑terminal alpha‑enolase (NAE) antibody was negative, as were antibodies associated with paraneoplastic neurological syndromes (anti‑amphiphysin, anti‑CV2, anti‑PNMA2, anti‑Ri, anti‑Yo, anti‑Hu, anti‑recoverin, anti‑SOX1, anti‑titin, anti‑zic4, anti‑GAD65, anti‑Tr/DNER).

Comprehensive malignancy screening—including upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy, mammography, pelvic MRI, and whole‑body contrast‑enhanced CT—did not reveal any tumors. Chest radiograph showed scattered calcified lesions in the left lower lung. Whole‑body CT demonstrated dilated bronchioles with granular, cord‑like, and plaque opacities in both lung apices. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed a mild pleocytosis (13 cells/µL; neutrophils 21 %, lymphocytes 68 %, histiocytes 11 %) with normal protein, glucose, and adenosine deaminase; oligoclonal bands were negative. PCR testing of CSF for common viruses (varicella‑zoster, HSV) was negative. CSF cytology was class I with no atypical cells. Bacterial, acid‑fast bacilli, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR cultures of CSF were negative, as were urine and sputum mycobacterial cultures. Head CT and brain MRI were unremarkable.

Positron emission tomography‑CT showed intense 18F‑fluorodeoxyglucose uptake in the hilar lymph nodes and left lung.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Autoimmune encephalopathy (Hashimoto’s encephalopathy) considered because of anti‑thyroid peroxidase positivity, but anti‑NAE antibody was negative, making the diagnosis unlikely. | "We considered Hashimoto's encephalopathy as a differential diagnosis, but the serum anti‑NH₂ terminal of alpha‑enolase (i.e., NAE) antibody test was negative."
2. Paraneoplastic neurological syndrome considered given the subacute cerebellar signs; extensive serum antibody panel was negative, reducing likelihood. | "anti‑amphiphysin ... antibody tests ... were negative."
3. Underlying malignancy as a cause of paraneoplastic syndrome was investigated; whole‑body imaging and endoscopic studies found no tumor. | "Upper and lower gastrointestinal endoscopy, mammography, pelvic magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), and whole‑body contrast‑enhanced computed tomography (CT) did not identify malignant tumors."
4. Viral encephalitis (HSV, VZV) considered; CSF PCR for these viruses was negative. | "Polymerase chain reaction tests for antimicrobials, varicella‑zoster virus, and herpes simplex virus (HSV) were negative."
5. Bacterial or fungal meningitis considered; CSF cell count was mildly elevated but protein, glucose, and cultures were normal, arguing against active infection. | "Cerebrospinal fluid examinations showed an elevated cell count ... but normal protein, glucose ... Bacterial culture, acid‑fast bacilli culture, and Mycobacterium tuberculosis PCR tests ... were negative."
6. Non‑tuberculous mycobacterial infection or disseminated TB considered; all CSF, urine, and sputum mycobacterial cultures were negative, but pulmonary imaging showed FDG‑avid lesions, raising suspicion for pulmonary TB. | "Positron emission tomography‑CT imaging ... showed significant 18F‑fluorodeoxyglucose accumulation in the hilar lymph nodes and left lung."
7. Pulmonary tuberculosis confirmed by bronchoalveolar lavage smear and culture for Mycobacterium tuberculosis (diagnostic test not yet presented in the prompt). | (Result presented after breakpoint in the full report.)

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case culminates in a diagnosis of primary cutaneous aspergillosis caused by Aspergillus fumigatus, which is on the SELECTED diseases list (aspergillosis). Therefore, the target diagnosis is **aspergillosis**.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: End the prompt just before the authors explicitly state “Therefore, the patient was given a diagnosis of PCA…”. Include the clinical presentation, tattoo history, diabetes, physical exam, negative HIV and other serologies, KOH findings, culture results, and histopathology (including PAS positivity) but omit the concluding diagnostic sentence.
3. Author's Analytic Distinctions: The authors distinguished aspergillosis from allergic/irritant dermatitis, eczema, and other cutaneous infections by (a) lack of response to antihistamines and topical steroids, (b) demonstration of septate hyaline hyphae on KOH, (c) growth of characteristic Aspergillus colonies on Sabouraud agar with MALDI‑TOF identification, and (d) PAS‑positive fungal spores in skin biopsy while systemic infection was excluded by normal laboratory work‑up.
case_prompt:
A 46‑year‑old woman presented with erythematous papules, papulopustules, and a plaque on the right lower limb that had been present for more than two years. She had previously been diagnosed with dermatitis and eczema at other hospitals and was treated with oral antihistamines (cetirizine, loratadine, ebastine) and topical glucocorticoids (mometasone furoate, halometasone) without improvement; the rash gradually enlarged. The patient’s past medical history was notable for type 2 diabetes mellitus for over 10 years, managed with metformin 0.5 g three times daily. Glycemic control had been satisfactory early on (fasting 6–7 mmol/L, postprandial 9–10 mmol/L) but later became poorly monitored; she recalled postprandial glucose values of 20–30 mmol/L around the time of tattooing and 13–15 mmol/L around lesion onset. She denied use of immunosuppressive agents or known immunodeficiency.

Physical examination showed only the cutaneous lesion on the right lower limb and red and blue‑black tattoos in the same area. HIV testing was negative. Routine blood work, T‑ and B‑cell subsets, renal and hepatic panels, treponemal serology, rapid plasma reagin, and immune indices (ANA, ENA, immunoglobulins, complement) were all within normal limits.

A potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation of the lesion revealed fungal hyphae. Tissue cultured on Sabouraud dextrose agar at 25 °C produced numerous dense grey‑black colonies. Microscopic examination of the colonies showed septate, hyaline hyphae with columnar conidia 2.5–3 µm in diameter, arising in chains from palisade‑like phialides directly attached to broadly clavate vesicles. Matrix‑assisted laser desorption/ionisation‑time of flight mass spectrometry identified the organism as *Aspergillus fumigatus*.

Skin biopsy demonstrated a reticulate cornified layer with oval spores within the corneous layer, a mildly thickened epidermis, and a sparse perivascular infiltrate of lymphocytes and neutrophils in the superficial dermis. Periodic acid‑Schiff staining was positive, and spores were visualized within the stratum corneum.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Initial diagnoses of dermatitis and eczema were considered because of the chronic papular and plaque‑like lesions, but the lack of response to antihistamines and topical glucocorticoids made these unlikely | "After the diagnoses of dermatitis and eczema, she was treated ... However, the lesions did not respond to treatment, and the rash gradually increased."
2. Bacterial skin infection was a possible alternative, yet routine cultures were not mentioned and the KOH preparation showed fungal hyphae, directing attention away from bacteria | "A KOH (potassium hydroxide) examination revealed visible fungal hyphae under the microscope."
3. Other cutaneous fungal infections (e.g., dermatophytes, Candida) were considered, but culture characteristics (dense grey‑black colonies, septate hyaline hyphae with columnar conidia, clavate vesicles) and MALDI‑TOF identified *A. fumigatus*, distinguishing it from dermatophytes or yeasts | "Numerous ... fungal colonies grew that were dense, and grey‑black... septate and hyaline hyphae with columnar conidia... identified as A. fumigatus."
4. Systemic immunodeficiency (e.g., HIV) could predispose to unusual infections, but HIV serology was negative and immune panels were normal, reducing this possibility | "The human immunodeficiency virus test was negative. Results of the laboratory tests for routine blood, T and B lymphocyte subpopulations ... were the normal range."
5. The presence of PAS‑positive spores in the stratum corneum confirmed a fungal etiology and, together with the culture, supported primary cutaneous aspergillosis while excluding deeper or disseminated infection | "Periodic acid‑Schiff staining was positive, and spores were observed in the cuticle."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient has a confirmed SARS‑CoV‑2 infection (COVID‑19), which is on the 21 SELECTED diseases list. Therefore the target diagnosis is **covid_19**.
2. Ideal Breakpoint: End the prompt just before the sentence that states the PCR result (“A polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test for COVID‑19 resulted positive”). All preceding clinical data (preceding respiratory symptoms, neurologic presentation, EMG, CSF, MRI, and negative serologies) give sufficient clues to suspect COVID‑19 while avoiding the explicit diagnostic spoiler.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors ruled out alternative causes of cerebral venous thrombosis (thrombophilia panel, antiphospholipid antibodies, ANCA, ACE, ENT disease) and other infectious etiologies (HIV, HCV, syphilis). They supported the diagnosis of COVID‑19‑associated Guillain‑Barre syndrome by the recent febrile respiratory prodrome, positive epidemiologic context, and later PCR confirmation, while electrophysiology and CSF findings confirmed an acute motor axonal polyradiculoneuropathy.
case_prompt:
A 66‑year‑old man with no prior medical history was admitted to the neurology department in September 2020 for bilateral peripheral facial palsy accompanied by an acute, symmetrical, proximal‑dominant tetraparesis and headache. Muscle strength was graded 3/5 proximally and 4/5 distally in the upper limbs and 1/5 proximally and 2/5 distally in the lower limbs. He was areflexic with numbness and tingling in all four limbs. The clinical picture suggested an acute polyradiculoneuropathy.  

One week before the neurological onset he experienced fever, dry cough, and vomiting. Given the prevailing epidemiologic situation, a viral respiratory infection was suspected.  

Electroneuromyography showed reduced motor amplitudes in all limbs, slightly slowed velocities, and absent F‑waves; sensory studies were normal, leading to a diagnosis of acute motor axonal polyradiculoneuropathy. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed albuminocytologic dissociation with a protein level of 1.38 g/L and normal cell count.  

Because of an acute headache, cerebral MRI with angiography was performed, demonstrating a cerebral venous thrombosis of the left sigmoid sinus.  

Standard laboratory tests (CBC, CRP, glucose, electrolytes, TSH, CK, urinalysis) were unremarkable. Serologies for HIV, hepatitis C, and treponemal disease were negative. An extensive work‑up for cerebral venous thrombosis—including ENT examination, pathergy test, thrombophilia panel (protein C, protein S, antithrombin III), antiphospholipid antibodies, p‑ANCA, c‑ANCA, ANA, and ACE—was negative.  

The patient was started on hydroxychloroquine (200 mg three times daily for 10 days), received five plasma‑exchange sessions, and was anticoagulated with low‑molecular‑weight heparin followed by a vitamin K antagonist.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Guillain‑Barre syndrome (acute motor axonal polyradiculoneuropathy) considered because of acute symmetrical tetraparesis, facial palsy, areflexia, and albuminocytologic dissociation in CSF. | "Electroneuromyography... reduced motor amplitude... absent F waves... Acute motor axonal polyradiculoneuropathy was diagnosed."
2. COVID‑19 infection considered due to prior fever, dry cough, vomiting, and epidemiologic context. | "He had fever, dry cough associated with vomiting one week before the onset of GBS symptoms. Given the existing epidemiological scenario and symptoms, COVID-19 infection was suspected."
3. Alternative infectious etiologies (HIV, hepatitis C, syphilis) ruled out by negative serologies. | "Standard laboratory tests ... and serologies (HIV, hepatitis C virus (HVC), treponema pallidum ... ) were also negative."
4. Thrombotic disorders (protein C/S deficiency, antithrombin III deficiency, antiphospholipid syndrome) excluded by normal thrombophilia panel. | "The thrombophilia assessment is unremarkable, in particular no deficiency in protein C, S, and antithrombin III."
5. Autoimmune vasculitis (ANCA‑associated) excluded by negative p‑ANCA, c‑ANCA, ANA, ACE. | "p ANCA, c ANCA antibodies, antinuclear antibodies (AAN), and angiotensin converting enzyme (ACE) were negative."
6. ENT sources of sinus thrombosis excluded by normal ENT examination. | "The examination of the ear, nose, and throat (ENT) sphere was normal."
7. COVID‑19 as the unifying cause was confirmed by positive PCR (although not disclosed in the prompt). | "A polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test for COVID-19 resulted positive."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The patient has confirmed brucellosis (Brucella abortus and Brucella melitensis serology) which is one of the 21 SELECTED diseases. Although acquired TTP is the primary focus of the report, the presence of sufficient clinical and laboratory data to diagnose brucellosis makes it the primary target diagnosis according to Rule 1.
2. Breakpoint: Include all information up to, but not including, the ADAMTS‑13 activity results and the definitive statement that the presentation is “specific to acquired TTP.” Thus the prompt ends after the report of Brucella serology and the initiation of doxycycline‑rifampin therapy.
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors initially considered immune‑mediated thrombocytopenia (ITP) and TTP, performed bone‑marrow studies, and evaluated infectious etiologies (viral, TB). The presence of non‑caseating granulomas prompted a broad infectious work‑up, leading to the identification of high‑titer Brucella antibodies; negative EBV/CMV/HIV and QuantiFERON‑TB excluded other common triggers. The response to anti‑brucellosis therapy, together with serology, supported brucellosis as the underlying cause.
case_prompt:
A 9‑year‑old previously healthy Syrian boy was admitted with a 1‑day history of epistaxis, hematemesis, hematuria, and melena associated with periumbilical abdominal pain. He had been complaining of pallor, decreased activity and appetite, and weight loss for the preceding month, with a noticeable increase in pallor one week before admission. On examination he was hypoactive, pale, and jaundiced; he was normothermic and hemodynamically stable. Systemic examination revealed hepatosplenomegaly and a small palpable lymph node in the supraclavicular and inguinal regions. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed bi‑cytopenia: platelet count 11 × 10⁹/L, hemoglobin 97 mg/L, white‑blood‑cell count 10.2 × 10⁹/L, and reticulocyte count 2.45 %. Peripheral smear demonstrated red‑blood‑cell fragmentation (schistocytes) at 1.45 % and neutrophilic toxic granulation. LDH was 1,021 U/L, AST 46 IU/L, ALP 143 IU/L, total bilirubin 41.3 µmol/L (direct 12.7 µmol/L). Urinalysis revealed hematuria and hemoglobinuria. Coagulation studies were normal; fibrinogen was 1.72 g/L. Coombs test was negative.

Initial management assumed atypical immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP); the patient received two doses of IVIG 1 g/kg without response, and platelet and hemoglobin levels continued to fall. Bone‑marrow aspiration and biopsy were performed; the aspirate showed megakaryocytes suggesting immune destruction, while the biopsy revealed frequent small epithelioid non‑necrotizing granulomas. Viral serologies for EBV, CMV, and HIV were negative, and QuantiFERON‑TB Gold was negative. Abdominal ultrasound and chest/abdominal CT demonstrated splenomegaly without significant lymphadenopathy.

Given the patient’s recent consumption of unpasteurized goat milk and cheese in a Brucella‑endemic region, Brucella serology was obtained and returned with titers of Brucella abortus 1:5,120 and Brucella melitensis 1:20,480 (both markedly elevated). A regimen of doxycycline (5 mg/kg orally twice daily) and rifampin (20 mg/kg orally twice daily) was started for six weeks. Following initiation of anti‑brucellosis therapy, the patient no longer required fresh frozen plasma transfusions, and his platelet and hemoglobin levels began to improve, with a concurrent decline in LDH.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) was considered because of isolated thrombocytopenia, but lack of response to IVIG and ongoing hemolysis made it unlikely. | "Initially, the patient was diagnosed with atypical idiopathic thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) and treated with Intravenous Immunoglobulin (IVIG) 1 g/kg. He received two doses of IVIG without response, and his Hgb and platelet counts declined further."
2. Thrombotic microangiopathy (including TTP) was entertained due to schistocytes and elevated LDH, prompting plasma exchange; however definitive ADAMTS‑13 data were not yet available at the breakpoint. | "The final result of BMA revealed peripheral destruction of blood cells, indicating microangiopathic hemolytic anemia (MAHA), likely TTP..."
3. Infectious triggers (viral EBV, CMV, HIV) were investigated because infections can precipitate MAHA; all tests were negative. | "Viral surveillance, including EBV, CMV, and HIV were negative."
4. Tuberculosis was evaluated given granulomatous bone‑marrow findings; QuantiFERON‑TB Gold was negative, reducing its likelihood. | "QuantiFERON‑TB Gold was negative."
5. Sarcoidosis was a differential for non‑caseating granulomas, but lack of pulmonary/lymph node enlargement and negative systemic findings made it less plausible. | "Considering that this is a nonspecific finding that could be attributed to various etiologies, including infections (viral, bacterial, and tuberculosis), infiltrating diseases such as sarcoidosis..."
6. Brucellosis emerged as a strong candidate because of endemic exposure (unpasteurized goat products) and markedly elevated serologic titers; initiation of doxycycline‑rifampin coincided with clinical improvement. | "Since Brucella is endemic in Saudi Arabia and the patient had recently consumed a significant amount of unpasteurized goat milk and cheese, brucella titers were sent, and the result showed Brucella abortus 1:5,120 ... Brucella melitensis 1:20,480... A combination of Doxycycline... and Rifampin... was commenced... Once starting the anti‑brucellosis management, the patient did not require further FFP transfusion... platelets count and hemoglobin levels recovered to the normal range."

case_analysis:
1. Target Diagnosis & Scope Check: The case focuses on pegfilgrastim‑induced aortitis, which is not among the 21 SELECTED diseases; therefore the diagnosis is OUT_OF_SCOPE.  
2. Ideal Breakpoint: Include the presentation up to the point where imaging showed aortic wall thickening and laboratory tests (ANCA, ANA) were negative, but stop before the authors state, “We suspected drug‑induced acute aortitis due to pegfilgrastim…” to avoid revealing the final diagnosis.  
3. Author’s Analytic Distinctions: The authors excluded infectious sources (negative cultures, no TB activity), ruled out classic large‑vessel vasculitides (giant cell arteritis, Takayasu) by ACR criteria, demonstrated negative ANCA and ANA serologies, and highlighted the temporal association with pegfilgrastim administration and rapid steroid response to support a drug‑induced vasculitis.
case_prompt:
A 71‑year‑old man with a history of rheumatoid arthritis treated with immunosuppressants and prednisolone underwent partial resection of left lower‑lobe large‑cell neuroendocrine carcinoma (stage IB) in December 201X. After a relapse in July 201X + 1, he received first‑course systemic chemotherapy (cisplatin and etoposide) in September 201X + 1, with pegfilgrastim given on day 4 because of concern for pulmonary tuberculosis relapse. He developed grade 1 fever on day 9; meropenem was started despite no evidence of infection. Grade 3 fever appeared on day 14 and persisted, reaching 40.3 °C on day 20. CRP rose in parallel with temperature. Contrast‑enhanced CT on day 21 showed no source of fever. Pyrazinamide was discontinued on day 21 for suspected drug‑induced fever, but fever continued, normalizing by day 28.

Second‑course chemotherapy began in November 201X + 1 with repeat pegfilgrastim on day 4. A grade 2 fever occurred on day 10, and on day 15 temperature peaked at 39.2 °C. Contrast‑enhanced CT on day 14 revealed new wall thickening of the aorta and left subclavian artery with perivascular contrast enhancement, not present before chemotherapy. No skin lesions or other organ symptoms were observed. Giant cell arteritis and Takayasu arteritis were considered but did not meet the American College of Rheumatology criteria. Blood tests were negative for MPO‑ANCA, PR3‑ANCA (chemiluminescent enzyme immunoassay), and antinuclear antibody (indirect fluorescent antibody method).
diagnostic_reasoning:

A 27‑year‑old man with trisomy 21 and intellectual disability presented with a 6‑month history of progressively worsening shortness of breath, productive cough, inspiratory stridor, night sweats, and recent voice loss, dysphagia, and choking on all consistencies. He had previously consulted nine physicians across ENT, pulmonology, gastroenterology, and allergy services in both Mexico and the United States and had received multiple courses of antibiotics for presumed pneumonia, antihistamines, inhaled bronchodilators, and systemic glucocorticoids without significant improvement. He denied diabetes, known immunodeficiency, or travel aside from brief trips to Mexico, and he regularly consumed unpasteurized dairy products from Mexico. Social history revealed residence with his mother in El Centro, California, frequent visits to an aunt in Mexicali, and exposure to areas with high prevalence of homelessness and illness; his mother denied known tuberculosis contacts.

An outside‑hospital computed tomography scan reported findings compatible with epiglottitis and a right upper‑lobe cavitary lung lesion, prompting transfer. On arrival he displayed inspiratory stridor, dysphonia, and dyspnea. Flexible fiberoptic laryngoscopy showed a boggy, edematous epiglottis with copious white frothy secretions and exophytic supraglottic masses that partially obstructed the airway. An awake tracheostomy was performed for airway stabilization, followed by direct laryngoscopy and bronchoscopy with biopsies. Intra‑operative inspection revealed diffuse firm, pseudo‑tumor‑like ulceroproliferative lesions involving the epiglottis, false vocal folds, ventricle, arytenoids, and true vocal folds. Flexible bronchoscopy demonstrated a normal tracheobronchial tree without lesions.

Histopathologic examination of the laryngeal tissue showed granulomatous inflammation with caseating necrosis, epithelioid histiocytes, chronic inflammatory cells, and multinucleated giant cells.

Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) was considered but deemed unlikely because of the patient’s epidemiologic exposure, presence of a cavitary lung lesion, normal admission CBC, and absence of sinonasal, renal, or cutaneous findings. | "Autoimmune causes such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) were considered; however, GPA was felt less likely given the patient's epidemiologic risk factors, cavitary lung lesion, normal admission CBC, and absence of sinonasal, renal, or cutaneous involvement."

Mycobacterial tuberculosis is supported by the combination of chronic constitutional symptoms, cavitary lung lesion, caseating granulomas on tissue histology, and high‑risk exposure (unpasteurized dairy, endemic region). | "A positive MTB‑RIF GeneXpert from the outside hospital and early biopsy histopathology showing caseating granulomas with a rare AFB further supported a mycobacterial etiology over autoimmune vasculitis."

case_prompt: A 54‑year‑old Sri Lankan man, six years post–live‑related renal transplantation, presented with progressive New York Heart Association class III dyspnea and abdominal distention of several months' duration. Physical examination revealed engorged jugular veins, tense ascites with tender hepatomegaly, and mild bilateral pitting edema of the ankles. Echocardiography demonstrated biatrial enlargement, left atrial diameter of 46 mm, normal‑size ventricles, good left ventricular function, and a dilated inferior vena cava (27 mm) with flow reversal. Paracentesis yielded transudate fluid. Subsequent cardiac catheterization displayed early, rapid diastolic filling and equalization of pressure between the ventricles consistent with constrictive pericarditis.

A 52‑year‑old previously healthy man was referred from a pneumology hospital in Yaoundé for evaluation of suspected heart failure. He reported shortness of breath on moderate exertion associated with a dry cough of two days duration, worse at night. He denied fever, weight loss, night sweats, chest pain, lower‑extremity swelling, or hemoptysis. Past history was unremarkable except for exposure to a patient with tuberculosis ten years ago; he was a never‑smoker and did not consume alcohol.

Physical examination: well‑built, no acute distress; blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, pulse 70/min, respiratory rate 19/min, temperature 36.9 °C, weight 71 kg, BMI 25.2 kg/m². Respiratory exam revealed clear breath sounds without wheezes or crackles. Cardiovascular exam showed a regular rhythm, no murmurs, no accentuation of the pulmonary component of the second heart sound, no jugular venous distension, and no peripheral edema.

Chest radiograph demonstrated an enlarged cardiac silhouette and a right middle‑lung lobe cavitary lesion with regional lymphadenopathy. ECG showed sinus rhythm, incomplete right bundle‑branch block, and T‑wave inversions in V1–V3. Echocardiography revealed a dilated right atrium and right ventricle, severe tricuspid regurgitation, and severe pulmonary artery hypertension with a pulmonary artery systolic pressure of 80 mmHg; left‑ventricular ejection fraction was 70 %.

case_prompt:
A 23‑year‑old female presented to the skin department with a large ulcer over the left side of the neck, as well as ulcers over the left axilla and chest wall that included a discharging sinus. She reported weight loss, loss of appetite, and intermittent fever. Two years earlier she had developed neck swellings for which she received Category II antituberculous therapy (ATT) for six months, without resolution; the swellings subsequently enlarged, and she was diagnosed with Rosai‑Dorfman syndrome and treated with systemic steroids for three months. 

On examination she looked ill, was malnourished, and anemic. There was matted cervical lymphadenopathy on the right side of the neck. An irregular ulcer 5 in × 3 in covering the left sternomastoid muscle had a slough‑covered floor; its base was indurated and formed by matted lymph nodes. Two additional irregular ulcers were present over the left axilla and chest wall, one with a discharging sinus, tethered to underlying indurated tissue. 

Clinically, multidrug‑resistant tuberculosis (TB), NTI, and immunodeficiency were considered as differentials. Hemogram showed anemia and an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate without leukocytosis. Touch smear and sputum were negative for tuberculous bacilli. Mantoux test was negative. Chest radiograph was normal. HIV I and II serology were negative. Pus culture grew Staphylococcus aureus. Biochemical parameters were normal. Histology revealed a lymphohistiocytic infiltrate in the dermis. She was empirically restarted on ATT Category II together with cotrimoxazole, but showed very little clinical response. Consequently, cultures were repeated; there was no growth from the discharge on blood agar, MacConkey agar and thioglycollate broth after 48 h of incubation.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Multidrug‑resistant TB considered due to chronic ulceration and prior ATT, but excluded because “Touch smear and sputum were negative for tuberculous bacilli,” “Mantoux test was negative,” and “There was very little clinical response to the above treatment.”  
2. Immunodeficiency (especially HIV) considered given non‑healing ulcers, but excluded as the patient was “negative for HIV I and II.”  
3. Common bacterial infection (Staphylococcus aureus) considered because “Pus culture grew Staphylococcus aureus,” yet excluded since “There was very little clinical response to the above treatment” with antibiotics and the ulcers persisted.  
4. Nontuberculous mycobacterial infection (NTI) remained plausible; definitive support came when “culture was repeated, which this time grew non pigmented, smooth colonies on Lowenstein‑Jensen medium on 7th day of inoculation at 37 °C,” and “The isolate reduced nitrate, was urease positive and sensitive to amikacin,” leading to molecular identification as “M. chelonae‑abscessus.”  
5. Successful targeted therapy with clarithromycin (“Within 2 weeks of institution of clarithromycin, the axillary ulcer and sinus healed… At the end of 40 days… the ulcer over the neck completely healed”) further confirmed the diagnosis.

case_prompt:
A 4‑year‑old boy from a rural area was brought to the Emergency Department with fever, severe persistent diffuse headache, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, and weight loss. The symptoms had been present for 4 months and worsened during the last week. His brother reported that the patient had suffered from recurrent respiratory infections since infancy with multiple hospital admissions. Two months earlier, after an MRI that suggested meningeal enhancement and small ring‑enhancing lesions, he had been started on antituberculosis therapy. He had no history of seizures or loss of consciousness. On examination the child was listless, emaciated, and extremely irritable, with left‑sided weakness of both the upper and lower extremities.

An urgent head CT showed multiple ring‑enhancing lesions in the left parieto‑occipital region with significant surrounding edema and mass effect. Laboratory studies revealed a white blood cell count of 17 900 µL (neutrophils 77.4 %, lymphocytes 15.7 %), hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL, and an erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 88 mm/h.

Neurosurgery performed a neuronavigation‑guided craniotomy with excision of the lesions. Thick purulent material was retrieved. Microscopic examination of the wall showed granulomas with fungal hyphae.

1. Aspergillosis suggested by demonstration of fungal hyphae in granulomatous brain lesions, which is characteristic of invasive Aspergillus infection in immunocompromised hosts. | "Microscopic examination revealed granulomas with fugal hyphae..."
2. Tuberculous meningoencephalitis considered because of prior MRI findings, ongoing antituberculosis therapy, and a family history of disseminated tuberculosis. | "Physicians ... started him on antituberculosis (ATT) drugs 2 months back after an MRI, which suggested meningeal enhancement and small ring enhancing lesions."
3. Bacterial brain abscess considered due to high peripheral white‑cell count, neutrophilia, and purulent material obtained at surgery. | "Thick purulent material" was obtained during craniotomy, and the leukocytosis (WBC 17 900, neutrophils 77.4 %) supports a bacterial process.
4. Neurocysticercosis ruled out because the lesions were described as ring‑enhancing with significant edema and mass effect, whereas cysticercal lesions typically lack such aggressive surrounding inflammation. | The imaging description emphasizes "multiple rings enhancing the left parietooccipital region, with significant surrounding edema and mass effect."
5. Pulmonary tuberculosis confirmed by PCR of tracheal aspirate, but the CNS lesions were attributed to Aspergillus rather than Mycobacterium tuberculosis owing to the presence of fungal hyphae. | "Tracheal aspirate ... was positive for Mycobacterium tuberculosis polymerase chain reaction assay."

case_prompt:
A 21‑year‑old man, working as a priest, presented with a 2‑year history of generalized raised nodular lesions. Two years ago he noticed small reddish lesions over the right knee that gradually enlarged and ruptured with blood‑stained purulent discharge. Similar lesions later appeared on the left knee, both elbows, and ears. The lesions were not associated with loss of sensation, pain, itching, burning, joint pain, swelling, or fever. He consulted a local doctor who performed a biopsy that was reported as suggestive of fungal infection; consequently he received itraconazole and amoxicillin‑clavulanic acid without improvement. No acid‑fast bacilli (AFB) staining was performed at that time.

On examination, multiple erythematous nodules and plaques ranging from 3 mm to 3 cm were present on the bilateral ear pinna and over bony prominences of the extremities (elbows, knees, malleoli, dorsal feet). Some lesions had hemorrhagic crusts. The nodules were nontender, firm to hard, without oozing, sinus formation, or ulceration. There was no known contact with leprosy patients.

Baseline blood tests were normal. Slit‑skin smears and biopsies from several lesions were obtained for bacterial and fungal cultures because subcutaneous mycoses were initially suspected. Microscopy and culture for both bacteria and fungi yielded negative results.

Standard nerve conduction studies demonstrated mild axonal sensory mononeuritis multiplex in the bilateral upper limbs and axonal sensory polyneuropathy in the bilateral lower limbs, with thickening of the greater auricular, ulnar, and common peroneal nerves.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Subcutaneous mycoses considered due to chronic nodular lesions; ruled out by lack of clinical response to itraconazole and negative fungal microscopy/culture. | "Microscopy as well as culture for both was negative."
2. Tuberculoid or other cutaneous mycobacterial infections considered; less likely because lesions were painless, chronic, and lacked ulceration, and initial biopsy suggested fungal rather than mycobacterial pathology. | "biopsy report was suggestive of fungal infection; hence, the patient was treated with itraconazole… without any relief."
3. Peripheral neuropathy (mononeuritis multiplex and polyneuropathy) pointed toward an infectious neuropathic process such as leprosy rather than pure fungal disease. | "Standard nerve stimulation test was done which showed evidence of mild axonal sensory mononeuritis multiplex… with bilateral greater auricular, ulnar, common peroneal nerves showing thickening."
4. Detection of numerous acid‑fast bacilli on modified Ziehl‑Neelsen stain confirmed Mycobacterium leprae infection, establishing leprosy. | "Examination of stained smear revealed characteristic AFB in large numbers… A bacterial index of 4+ (10 AFB per oil immersion field) was recorded."
5. Histopathology showing diffuse polymorphous infiltrate with foamy histiocytes and AFB highlighted by Fite‑Faraco stain corroborated leprosy and excluded fungal organisms. | "AFB were highlighted by Fite‑Faraco stain…"

case_prompt:
A 25‑year‑old man from a middle‑class background presented with a one‑month history of abdominal pain, abdominal distention, and fever. He denied joint pain, gastrointestinal bleeding, cough, dyspnea, chest pain, palpitations, facial edema, urinary symptoms, jaundice, and had normal bowel habits. On examination he appeared ill, was anemic and icteric, but was well oriented. He had average build, no bony tenderness, lymphadenopathy, or organomegaly. There was ascites with sluggish bowel sounds; liver dullness was not obliterated. No edema, flapping tremor, or stigmata of chronic liver disease were noted. 2. Malaria considered but excluded by negative peripheral smear | "He tested negative for ... malarial parasite."
3. Leishmaniasis considered but excluded by negative rk39 test | "He tested negative for ... RK39."
4. Autoimmune liver disease considered but excluded by negative ANA and ASMA | "He tested negative for ANA, ASMA."

Tuberculous peritonitis considered despite negative tuberculin skin test and low ADA because of lymphocyte‑predominant high‑protein ascites, hepatosplenomegaly, and lack of alternative diagnoses | "Ascitic fluid showed lymphocytes 95% ... protein 38 gm/l ... ADA 22.6 U/l." and "He was identified as a tuberculosis (TB) suspect."

case_prompt:
A 5‑year‑old boy from rural Sabah presented with a one‑month history of headache, right eye pain, vomiting, difficulty walking, blurred vision, and fluctuating consciousness, accompanied by weight loss and anorexia. He had received BCG vaccination but missed other immunizations. On exam his GCS was 9 (E2V2M5), he had left lateral strabismus, unequal sluggish pupils (4 mm/3 mm), and symmetric 4/5 strength in all limbs with normal reflexes; Babinski was downgoing and Kernig’s sign was absent.

Non‑contrast CT showed acute hydrocephalus with cerebral edema, and an external ventricular drain was placed, revealing high opening pressure and clear CSF. MRI demonstrated diffuse enhancing nodular leptomeningeal thickening, especially at the basal cisterns, without intra‑axial lesions; small non‑enhancing cystic lesions were noted along the leptomeningeal surface.

A tuberculous meningitis work‑up was performed. ESR was 90 mm/h and CSF protein was elevated with normal glucose. Mantoux test was negative; blood, CSF, and CSF cultures were negative for organisms. CSF acid‑fast bacilli smear, CSF GeneXpert, and gastric lavage smear and GeneXpert were all negative. CSF latex agglutination was negative for Group B Streptococcus, Haemophilus influenzae, Streptococcus pneumoniae, Neisseria meningitidis, and Escherichia coli. Using Composite Reference Standard criteria the child was classified as probable TB and started on isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, ethionamide, and dexamethasone.

After 14 days his condition improved, and ophthalmology showed right visual acuity 1/60 and no light perception in the left eye with a positive afferent pupillary defect. He was discharged after a 4‑week stay.

One month later he returned with vomiting, unsteady gait, and anorexia. Repeat MRI showed markedly more extensive nodular leptomeningeal enhancement and enlargement of the previously seen cystic lesions. MR spectroscopy of the thickened tentorium cerebelli revealed a markedly elevated choline:creatine ratio of 4.34 and absence of a singlet peak at 3.8 ppm. A transcranial biopsy was performed during revision of his external ventricular shunt, and dural tissue was obtained for analysis.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Tuberculous meningitis was initially favored because of diffuse leptomeningeal enhancement, high ESR, and elevated CSF protein. | "A diagnosis of tuberculous meningitis was considered, and an extensive TB workup was undertaken."
2. Overt TB infection was deemed unlikely due to multiple negative microbiologic tests. | "The Mantoux test was negative, and the blood, CSF, and CSF TB cultures showed no organism... The CSF for acid‑fast bacilli as well as CSF GeneXpert were also negative."
3. Bacterial meningitis was excluded by negative CSF latex agglutination for common pathogens. | "CSF latex agglutination was negative for streptococcus Group B, haemophilus influenzae, streptococcus pneumoniae, neisseria meningitidis, and escherichia coli."
4. Smear‑negative TB remained a provisional diagnosis, classified as probable TB by CRS criteria, but clinical relapse despite therapy prompted further investigation. | "Smear‑negative TB was considered after reviewing the biochemical and imaging findings. Using the Composite Reference Standard (CRS) criteria, this child was classified as probable TB."
5. Histopathology of the dural biopsy demonstrated a highly proliferative, S100‑ and synaptophysin‑positive neoplasm, establishing a diffuse leptomeningeal glioneuronal tumor. | "Immunohistochemical (IHC) studies showed that the tumor cells were positive for S100 and synaptophysin... Given these findings, the boy was diagnosed with DL‑GNT."

case_prompt:
A 62‑year‑old woman was admitted with nine days of paroxysmal falls and impaired consciousness and four days of paroxysmal limb twitching with gibberish speech. Initial tonic‑clonic seizures progressed to frequent tonic seizures with right‑ward head turning, resembling faciobrachial dystonic seizures, occurring >10 times per day. Prior brain MRI was normal. Initial antiseizure therapy (sodium valproate, diazepam, levetiracetam) yielded no improvement. She denied hypertension, coronary disease, diabetes, cerebrovascular disease, mental illness, hepatitis, tuberculosis, and had no family history of hereditary disease.

On admission: temperature 36.3 °C, heart rate 91 /min, respiratory rate 20/min, blood pressure 162/85 mmHg. Neurologic exam showed cognitive dysfunction (poor memory, poor calculation) with otherwise normal cranial nerves, motor strength, reflexes, sensation, coordination, gait, and no meningeal signs.

Routine blood tests, coagulation, liver and kidney panels, glucose, lipids, serology for hepatitis B, syphilis, HIV, ANA, ANCA, rheumatoid factor, thyroid antibodies, and tumor markers were all normal except low serum chloride (95 mmol/L). Serum auto‑immune encephalitis panel was notable only for anti‑LGI1 antibody titer 1:16 (normal < 1:10); all other neuronal antibodies (NMDAR, CASPR2, GABABR, DPPX, GAD65) and paraneoplastic antibodies were negative.

CSF analysis showed slight lymphocytic leukocytosis (10 × 10⁶/L) with normal opening pressure, appearance, glucose, chloride, Gram stain, acid‑fast stain, ink stain, metagenomic NGS, and CSF neuronal antibodies. CSF treponemal testing was positive (TPPA) and non‑treponemal testing (RPR) was positive.

Serum rapid plasma reagin (RPR) was positive at 1:16 and TPPA positive. CSF TPPA and RPR were also positive.

EEG demonstrated irregular medium‑ to high‑amplitude slow waves with occasional sharp waves in the right temporal lobe, spreading bilaterally. Brain MRI revealed increased T2/FLAIR signal in the medial right temporal lobe with mild‑moderate gadolinium enhancement; magnetic resonance angiography was normal. Chest CT, echocardiography, abdominal and urinary ultrasounds, electromyography, and nerve conduction studies were unremarkable.

1. Neurosyphilis supported by serologic evidence: positive serum RPR (1:16) and TPPA, and concordant positive CSF TPPA and RPR, indicating intrathecal treponemal infection. | "The patient had a positive RPR with a serum titer of 1:16 and a positive TPPA. Subsequently, TPPA and RPR in CSF were tested, and both results were positive."
2. Anti‑LGI1 encephalitis considered due to serum anti‑LGI1 antibody (1:16) and limbic‑type seizures, but CSF LGI1 antibodies were absent and CSF pleocytosis was mild, making isolated autoimmune encephalitis less certain. | "serum ... anti‑LGI1 antibody with a titer of 1:16... The CSF showed slight leukocytosis ... AE‑related antibodies ... were normal."
3. Viral encephalitis (e.g., HSV, VZV) excluded by negative CSF metagenomic NGS, negative Gram/acid‑fast/ink stains, and lack of fever or classic imaging pattern. | "metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS), ... Gram staining, acid‑fast staining, ink staining ... were normal."
4. HIV‑associated neurocognitive disorder ruled out by negative HIV serology. | "serological testing for ... HIV were negative."
5. Tuberculous meningitis excluded by negative acid‑fast stain, absence of typical CSF findings, and normal chest imaging. | "acid‑fast staining ... were normal" and "CT of the chest ... were normal."
6. Paraneoplastic limbic encephalitis excluded by negative tumor markers and absent onconeural antibodies (anti‑Hu, anti‑Ri, anti‑Yo, etc.). | "serum tumor markers ... were normal" and "PNS‑related antibodies ... were normal."

Primary anti‑LGI1 encephalitis alone deemed possible but overlapping with neurosyphilis because both can produce limbic MRI changes and seizures; the presence of intrathecal treponemal antibodies tipped the balance toward neurosyphilis as the primary driver. | "Uncertainty arose as to whether the patient had both anti‑LGI1 encephalitis and NS or whether the LGI1 antibody and LE manifestations were due to the NS."

case_prompt: A 65‑year‑old man with a remote history of left radical nephrectomy for clear cell renal cell carcinoma (ccRCC) in 2002 and a recent diagnosis of stage II diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma (DLBCL) treated with three cycles of R‑CHOP and consolidative radiotherapy presented in 2020 with non‑neutropenic fevers and rigors of unclear source. After a second dose of combination immune‑checkpoint inhibition (ipilimumab 1 mg/kg plus nivolumab 3 mg/kg), he returned to the emergency department with persistent fevers, acute kidney injury, and transaminitis. Broad‑spectrum antibiotics and isavuconazole were administered because of known pulmonary nodules. Imaging revealed new generalized lymphadenopathy in the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and diffusely avid splenomegaly on PET/CT. Differential diagnoses included recurrence of DLBCL, hyperprogression of metastatic ccRCC, immune‑related toxicity with a sarcoid‑like reaction, or other infectious/inflammatory causes. A left axillary fine‑needle aspirate and core biopsy showed granulomatous inflammation; stains for mycobacteria (Ziehl‑Neelsen) and fungi (GMS) were negative, and no malignant cells were identified. An extensive infectious work‑up was negative, including T‑spot, AFB blood cultures, coccidioides serologies, Q fever serologies, Bartonella serologies, blood histoplasma antigen, and histoplasma antibody. Given his farm exposures and splenic granulomata, histoplasmosis was considered despite negative serologies, while a sarcoid‑like reaction was also entertained but steroids were withheld because pulmonary function tests were normal and there were no parenchymal lung findings.

case_prompt: A 16‑year‑old male student from Jieyang City, Guangdong Province was admitted on 11 November 2020 with a 6‑month history of intermittent dry cough without fever, chest pain, or known exposures to birds or soil. Chest CT performed on 19 October at a local hospital showed a lung shadow suspicious for tuberculosis, prompting referral. On admission, physical examination was unremarkable. Laboratory tests revealed a white blood cell count of 7.20 × 10⁹/L, neutrophils 51.9 % (3.73 × 10⁹/L), and C‑reactive protein 9 mg/L. Both T‑SPOT and purified protein derivative (PPD) skin test were positive (13 × 14 mm). Serial sputum acid‑fast stains on 13, 14, and 15 November were negative. A chest plain film and contrast‑enhanced CT on 13 November demonstrated cavitary lesions in the left lower lobe and right lung, interpreted as possible pyogenic inflammation, fungal infection, or secondary tuberculosis. Empiric cefotaxime‑sulbactam 2.25 g intravenously twice daily was started. After 10 days, repeat CT showed little change. Immunoglobulin levels, T‑cell subsets, and HIV testing were normal. Bronchoscopy on 17 November displayed congested and edematous bronchial mucosa throughout both lungs; bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) cytology showed respiratory epithelium and few neutrophils, without malignant cells. Tracheoscopic brushings were similarly non‑diagnostic. BALF GeneXpert for Mycobacterium tuberculosis was negative, as were tests for MTB‑DNA and rpoB; the (1→3)-β‑D‑glucan assay was <37.5 pg/mL. No acid‑fast bacilli, bacteria, spores, or hyphae were observed microscopically. A second bronchoscopy on 20 November confirmed bilateral bronchitis, and BALF was sent for metagenomic next‑generation sequencing (mNGS).

Tuberculosis considered due to positive T‑SPOT, positive PPD, and cavitary lesions on imaging; excluded because multiple sputum smears and GeneXpert were negative and there was no radiographic response after anti‑tuberculous‑suspicion treatment. | "T‑SPOT and pure protein derivative (PPD) skin test (13 × 14 mm) were positive... GeneXpert (-): MTB‑DNA: negative, rpoB: negative."
2. Bacterial pyogenic pneumonia suggested by cavitary lesions and initial empiric cefotaxime‑sulbactam; excluded because after 10 days of appropriate antibiotics, chest CT showed little change and cultures remained negative. | "After 10 days of regular treatment, the chest CT scan showed little change compared with pre‑treatment."
3. Common fungal infection (e.g., Aspergillus) entertained given cavitary lesions; G test was negative and microscopy showed no hyphae, lowering this possibility. | "G test revealed <37.50 pg/ml. No acid‑fast bacilli, bacteria, spores, or hyphae were found."
4. Malignancy considered during bronchoscopy; cytology of BALF and brushings showed no cancer cells, effectively ruling it out. | "Microscopic examination of bronchial lavage fluid (BALF) ... no cancer cells."
5.
